Introducing Linear Implication Types to λ G ​ T \lambda_{GT} for Computing With Incomplete Graphs
Jin Sano, Naoki Yamamoto, Kazunori Ueda

Abstract
Designing programming languages that enable intuitive and safe manipulation of data structures is a critical research challenge. Conventional destructive memory operations using pointers are complex and prone to errors. Existing type systems, such as affine types and shape types, address this problem towards safe manipulation of heaps and pointers, but design of high-level declarative languages that allow us to manipulate complex pointer data structures at a higher level of abstraction is largely an open problem. The λ G ​ T \lambda_{GT} language, a purely functional programming language that treats hypergraphs (hereafter referred to as graphs) as primary data structures, addresses some of these challenges. By abstracting data with shared references and cycles as graphs, it enables declarative operations through pattern matching and leverages its type system to guarantee safety of these operations. Nevertheless, the previously proposed type system of λ G ​ T \lambda_{GT} leaves two significant open challenges. First, the type system does not support incomplete graphs , that is, graphs in which some elements are missing from the graphs of user-defined types. Second, the type system relies on dynamic type checking during pattern matching. This study addresses these two challenges by incorporating linear implication into the λ G ​ T \lambda_{GT} type system, while introducing new constraints to ensure its soundness.

1
Introduction

Designing programming languages that enable intuitive and safe manipulation of complex data structures
remains a fundamental challenge in programming language research.
Traditional destructive
pointer manipulation introduce
complexity and are susceptible to errors
such as memory leaks and dangling references.
To address these issues, various type systems have been
proposed, including affine/linear types
for ensuring compile-time memory safety and shape types

[
9
]
for
representing pointer data structures with sharing and cycles.
Whereas imperative programs with explicit manipulation of heaps
and pointers could benefit from them, design of high-level declarative
languages that allow us to manipulate pointer data structures at a
higher level of abstraction is largely an open problem.

The
\lambda_{GT}
language
offers a novel approach to addressing these challenges
[
28
,
27
]
.
In
\lambda_{GT}
,
data structures with shared references and cycles are abstracted as

port hypergraphs
,
a generalisation of graphs in which a hyperedge can connect any number of nodes
by attaching to them at specific points called
ports
.
The
\lambda_{GT}
language is
a purely functional language that
supports port hypergraphs (hereafter referred to as graphs)
as primary data structures,
providing declarative manipulation of these structures
based on
graph decomposition through pattern matching

and
construction of new graphs based on graph composition

(as opposed to explicit, step-by-step pointer manipulation).
Moreover,
\lambda_{GT}
is equipped with a type system that allows users
to define structural constraints and enforces that all values
strictly conform to these user-defined specifications.
Nevertheless, the previously proposed type system of
\lambda_{GT}

leaves two significant open challenges.

First, the type system does not support
incomplete graphs
,
that is, graphs in which some elements are missing from the graphs of user-defined types.
For example, a doubly-linked list missing one or more tail nodes and a leaf-linked tree with one or more absent leaves
cannot be properly captured by the previous type system.
Such incomplete graphs naturally arise in practice,
particularly in pattern matching.
Although users may define separate types for such incomplete structures, this approach is cumbersome and lacks generality.

Second, the type system relies on dynamic type checking during pattern matching.
Although this mechanism guarantees type soundness,
achieving fully static type checking remains an important open challenge.

This study addresses these open challenges
by incorporating
linear implication types

into the
\lambda_{GT}
type system,
enabling static typing of incomplete graphs.
We have found that a naive integration of linear implication types leads to unsoundness in certain scenarios.
To overcome this, we propose additional constraints on both the type system and the language syntax.

1.1
Contributions

This paper makes the following contributions:

1.

We propose a novel type system that incorporates linear implications
into the previous type system of
\lambda_{GT}

to enable static checking of pattern matching with incomplete graphs (
Section

3
).

2.

We identify an issue where the naive application of linear implications leads to unsoundness
(
Section

4.1.1
).

3.

To ensure soundness,
we introduce additional constraints on production rules in the type system
and patterns in case expressions (
Section

4.2
).

1.2
Structure of the Paper

The remainder of this paper is structured as follows.

Section

2
presents an overview of the
\lambda_{GT}
language,
including its syntax, semantics, and type system,
and identifies open problems that remain to be addressed.

Section

3
describes our proposed extension to the

\lambda_{GT}
type system
that incorporates linear implications,
and discusses its properties with
a complete proof of soundness (under dynamic type checking in
case expressions) (our first contribution).
It also gives some typing examples and
discussion on the admissibility of typing rules.

Section

4
examines the soundness of the extended type system
(without dynamic checking),
highlighting counterexamples that reveal the limitations of naive approaches
(our second contribution),
presents the constraints we propose to address these issues
(our third contribution),
and discusses the soundness under extended typing rules.

Section

5
discusses related work,
comparing our approach with existing verification frameworks and type systems for graphs and data structures.

Section

6
concludes the paper and outlines possible directions for future research.

Preliminaries

We introduce some syntactic conventions as follows:

\overrightarrow{E}
denotes

E_{1},\dots,E_{n}

or

E_{1}\dots E_{n}

for some
n\ (\geq 0)
and
some syntactic entity

E_{i}\ (1\leq i\leq n)
.
The length
n
of
\overrightarrow{E}
is denoted as
\lvert\overrightarrow{E}\rvert
.

S\{s\}
denotes a set
S

such that
s\in S
.
Hypergraphs and hyperlinks (hyperedges) may be simply denoted as graphs and links, respectively.

2
The
\lambda_{GT}
Language

This section presents an overview of
\lambda_{GT}
,
a purely functional programming language
that integrates hypergraphs and their transformations into the functional programming paradigm
[
28
]
.
In
\lambda_{GT}
, data structures are represented as hypergraphs,
enabling computations to be expressed via graph transformations
[
5
,
23
]
.
In contrast to traditional imperative approaches that rely on destructive pointer-based memory operations,
which are often both complex and error-prone,

\lambda_{GT}
employs compositional constructs and graph pattern matching.
This design ensures fully declarative manipulation of data structures.
Another key feature of
\lambda_{GT}
is its type system,
which guarantees safety and ensures that operations preserve user-defined structural forms.

The core design requirements for the
\lambda_{GT}
language are as follows:

1.

The language should allow graphs to be composed easily.

2.

The language should allow variables to be bound to graphs.

3.

The language should support graph decomposition via pattern matching.

4.

As a functional language, it should treat functions as
first-class citizens
(possibly with lightweight mechanism for embedding functions
into graph structures and taking functions out of graph structures).

We first describe the syntax and semantics of
\lambda_{GT}
in
Section

2.1
,
which addresses all these requirements.

Further requirements for the type system are as follows:

5.

The type system should allow users to define the types of graph structures
and be able to verify that values conform to these types.

6.

The type system should be able to handle intermediate forms of graph structures
during manipulations.

7.

The type system is expected to be fully static.

We describe the existing type system in
Section

2.2
.
Although the type system satisfies Requirement 5,
Requirements 6 and 7 remain open challenges,
as highlighted in previous work and described in
Section

2.3
.

For further details of
\lambda_{GT}
not described in full below,
the readers are referred to
[
28
]
.

2.1
Syntax and Semantics

The syntax of
\lambda_{GT}
consists of
two mutually dependent ingredients:
(i) term-based hypergraph representations as values
and (ii) expressions that manipulate these structures.
To realise Requirement 1,
we adopt the graph definition style of HyperLMNtal
[
25
,
26
]
,
which offers both a term-based syntax and compositional semantics.

definitions of HyperLMNtal
have been extended and adapted into a functional language framework
in a mutually dependent manner.

In
\lambda_{GT}
,
values are hypergraphs,
which are written in a term-based syntax
to ensure
high affinity with programming languages
[
26
]
.

•

The term
\mathbf{0}
denotes the empty graph.

•

An
atom

p(\overrightarrow{X})

stands for a
node
of a data structure with the label
p
and
totally ordered links
\overrightarrow{X}
.
The individual links are regarded as attached to

ports
(
1^{\textrm{st}}
,
2^{\textrm{nd}}
,
\dots
)
of an atom rather than the atom itself, and such
(hyper)graphs are often called
port (hyper)graphs
.

An atom name
(i.e., a node label)
is either a constructor
(as in
\mathrm{Nil}(X)
and

\mathrm{Cons}(Y,Z,X)
)
or a
\lambda
-abstraction.

A
\lambda
-abstraction atom has the form

(\lambda\,x[\overrightarrow{X}].e)(\overrightarrow{Y})
.
Here,
x[\overrightarrow{X}]
,
where
\overrightarrow{X}
is a sequence of

pairwise distinct
links,
denotes a
graph variable
,
which corresponds to and extends
a variable in functional languages.
We need this extension
(with the
[\overrightarrow{X}]
)
because, unlike standard tree structures
with single roots, a graph
may have an arbitrary number of roots
that are “access points” to
the graph from outside.

The
\lambda
-abstraction atom

(\lambda\,x[\overrightarrow{X}].e)(\overrightarrow{Y})

takes a graph with free links
(i.e., links not hidden by
\nu X
described soon below)

\overrightarrow{X}
,
binds it to the graph variable
x[\overrightarrow{X}]
, and
returns the value
obtained by evaluating the expression
e

with the bound graph variable.
The
\overrightarrow{Y}
attached to the abstraction represent the links
of the atom whose name (node label) is the abstraction.
Those links are used for forming graph structures containing
functions but becomes unnecessary and disappears upon

\beta
-reduction (as will be defined in
\figref
table:lgt-reduction).

•

A
fusion
,

X\bowtie Y
,
fuses the link
X
and the link
Y
into a single link.

•

A
molecule
,

(G,G)
,
stands for
the composition or gluing of graphs.

•

A
hyperlink creation
,

\nu X.G
, hides the link name
X
in
G
.
In
\lambda_{GT}
, all links are

free links
as long as they are not hidden.
The set of free links in
T
is denoted as
\mathit{fn}(T)

defined inductively as in
\figref
table:free-names.

\displaystyle\mathit{fn}(\textbf{0})

\displaystyle\triangleq\emptyset

\displaystyle\mathit{fn}(p(\overrightarrow{X}))

\displaystyle\triangleq\{\overrightarrow{X}\}

\displaystyle\mathit{fn}(X\bowtie Y)

\displaystyle\triangleq\{X,Y\}

\displaystyle\mathit{fn}((T_{1},T_{2}))

\displaystyle\triangleq\mathit{fn}(T_{1})\cup\mathit{fn}(T_{2})

\displaystyle\mathit{fn}(\nu X.T)

\displaystyle\triangleq\mathit{fn}(T)\setminus\{X\}

\displaystyle\mathit{fn}(x[\overrightarrow{X}])

\displaystyle\triangleq\{\overrightarrow{X}\}

Figure 3:
The set of free link names

Links that do not occur free are called
local links
.

Since values are represented as graphs, and graphs may include

\lambda
-abstractions as node labels,
the language
naturally supports higher-order programming.
Furthermore, values can be graphs containing one or more
\lambda
-abstractions.
This allows the representation of not only lists or trees of functions
(as in standard functional languages)
but also
dataflow graphs with functions assigned to each node,
as demonstrated in
[
27
]
.

A
\lambda_{GT}

program is called an
expression

which is either of the following:

•

T
is a graph with zero or more graph variables.

•

(\mathbf{case}\;e_{1}\;\mathbf{of}\;T\to e_{2}\;\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to e_{3})

evaluates
e_{1}
,
checks whether it matches the graph template
T
, and
reduces to
e_{2}
or
e_{3}
.
We require that
graph variables names occurring in pattern
T

are pairwise distinct
and that
the link names in each
graph variables are pairwise distinct.

•

(e_{1}\;e_{2})
is an application.

Definition 2.2

(Syntactic Convention)
.

For convenience, we introduce some abbreviation rules.

1.

An atom
p()
(with no arguments) is written also as
p
.

2.

A sequence of nested
binders

\nu X_{1}.\,\dots\,.\nu X_{n}.T

can be abbreviated to

\nu X_{1}\dots X_{n}.T

or
\nu\overrightarrow{X}.T
.
When
n=0
,
\nu.T
is written also as
T
.

3.

The
term notation
allows

\nu Y.(p_{1}(\overrightarrow{X},Y,\overrightarrow{Z}),p_{2}(\overrightarrow{W},Y)),

where
Y\notin\{\overrightarrow{X},\overrightarrow{Z},\overrightarrow{W}\}
,
to be written as

p_{1}(\overrightarrow{X},p_{2}(\overrightarrow{W}),\overrightarrow{Z}).

That is, an atom
p_{2}(\overrightarrow{W},Y)
may be embedded into the
position of the other occurrence of
Y
as
p_{2}(\overrightarrow{W})
.
Here, we allow
\overrightarrow{X},\overrightarrow{Z},\overrightarrow{W}
to contain such embedded
atoms (rather than links) introduced by the term notation.

4.

As in other functional languages,
we provide the form

\mathbf{let}\;x[\overrightarrow{X}]\;\texttt{=}\;e^{\prime}\;\mathbf{in}\;e

as an abbreviation for

((\lambda\,x[\overrightarrow{X}].e)()\;e^{\prime})
,
which can be written also (by (1)) as

((\lambda\,x[\overrightarrow{X}].e)\;e^{\prime})
.

∎

An example of the term notation will be given as soon as
Structural Congruence is introduced in
Definition

2.3
.

We introduce two forms of
substitution in
\lambda_{GT}
.

Link substitution

\sigma
replaces occurrences of free link names within a graph with
other link names.
For example,
T\langle\overrightarrow{Z}/\overrightarrow{Y}\rangle
denotes the substitution of all
free occurrences of
\overrightarrow{Y}
in
T
with
\overrightarrow{Z}
.

Graph substitution

\theta
replaces occurrences of free graph variables within an
expression with specified
graph( template)s.
For example,
e[T/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]
denotes the replacement of all
occurrences of
x[\overrightarrow{X}]
in the expression
e
with the graph template

T
.
We require that the link names in
\overrightarrow{X}
are pairwise distinct and
also that
\mathit{fn}(T)=\{\overrightarrow{X}\}
, that is, the substitution does not
change the set of free links.
Their formal definitions, which avoid capture
(of local links or local graph variables) in a standard manner,
can be found in Appendix
A
.

To establish a formal foundation for pattern matching,
we introduce the equivalence relation
\equiv
on graphs
and graph templates.

Definition 2.3

(Structural Congruence)
.

The equivalence relation
\equiv
on graphs
and graph templates is defined as the minimal equivalence relation
that satisfies the rules given in
\figref
table:lgt-cong.
∎

(E1)
(\mathbf{0},T)\equiv T

(E2)
(T_{1},T_{2})\equiv(T_{2},T_{1})

(E3)
(T_{1},(T_{2},T_{3}))\equiv((T_{1},T_{2}),T_{3})

(E4)
\dfrac{T_{1}\equiv T_{2}}{(T_{1},T_{3})\equiv(T_{2},T_{3})}

(E5)
\dfrac{T_{1}\equiv T_{2}}{\nu X.T_{1}\equiv\nu X.T_{2}}

(E6)
\nu X.(X\bowtie Y,T)\equiv\nu X.T\langle Y/X\rangle

where
X\in\mathit{fn}(T)\lor Y\in\mathit{fn}(T)

(E7)
\nu X.\nu Y.X\bowtie Y\equiv\mathbf{0}

(E8)
\nu X.\mathbf{0}\equiv\mathbf{0}

(E9)
\nu X.\nu Y.T\equiv\nu Y.\nu X.T

(E10)
\nu X.(T_{1},T_{2})\equiv(\nu X.T_{1},T_{2})

where
X\notin\mathit{fn}(T_{2})

Figure 4:
Congruence Rules Over
\lambda_{GT}
Graph Templates.

Two graphs related by
\equiv
are essentially the same and are convertible
to each other in zero steps.
(E1), (E2) and (E3) are the characterisation of molecules as multisets.
(E4) and (E5) are structural rules that make
\equiv
a congruence.
(E6) and (E7) are concerned with fusions.
(E7) says that a closed fusion is equivalent to
\mathbf{0}
.
(E6) is an absorption law of
\bowtie
,
which says that a fusion can be absorbed by connecting hyperlinks.
Because of the symmetry of
\equiv
,
(E6) says that a graph can emit a fusion as well.
For the symmetry of
\bowtie
,
we refer the reader to Theorem 2.1 in
[
28
]
.
(E8), (E9) and (E10) are concerned with hyperlink creation.

(Term Notation)
.

Consider

\begin{array}[]{l@{\qquad}l}\nu Z_{1}.\nu Z_{2}.\nu Z_{3}.\nu Z_{4}.(&\\
\quad\mathrm{Node}(Z_{1},Z_{2},X),&(a_{1})\\
\quad\quad\mathrm{Node}(Z_{3},Z_{4},Z_{1}),&(a_{2})\\
\quad\qquad\mathrm{Leaf}(Z_{3}),&(a_{3})\\
\quad\qquad\mathrm{Leaf}(Z_{4}),&(a_{4})\\
\quad\quad\mathrm{Leaf}(Z_{2}),&(a_{5})\\
).\end{array}

Since structural congruence allows the reordering of atoms
(E2)(E3) and the reordering and movement of binders (E9)(E10),
the term notation (

(3))
allows us to write the above graph as

by embedding

and

into

and then embedding

and
a_{5}
into

.

Rd-Case1
and

are for

If the matching has succeeded (
Rd-Case1
),

the graph substitution obtained in the matching.

Rd-

2.1.1
Motivating Examples

In the
\lambda_{GT}
language,
it is possible to express transformations on data structures
such as removing the last element from a doubly-linked list or applying a function to
the leaves of a leaf-linked tree in a purely declarative manner.
These transformations rely on pattern matching and avoid the need for explicit
destructive updates to the heap or pointer manipulations.

A doubly-linked list is a fundamental data structure frequently used in programming
due to its efficiency in supporting bidirectional traversal.
In
\lambda_{GT}
, a doubly-linked list is naturally represented as a graph,
where each
\mathrm{Cons}
node maintains hyperlinks (i.e., pointers) to both its predecessor and successor nodes,
and a
\mathrm{Nil}
node terminates the list.
The formal encoding of a doubly-linked list in this language is given as follows:
Here,
the first argument of each
\mathrm{Cons}
atom is connected to its value;
for example,
1,2
, and
3
.
The second and the third argument point to the previous and next elements,
respectively.
The last argument is the access point to the current node,
which also applies to the
\mathrm{Nil}
node.
The first argument of the
\mathrm{Nil}
node points to the previous node.

\displaystyle G_{\mathsf{DL3}}\triangleq\begin{array}[]{lll}\nu W_{1}W_{2}W_{3}W_{4}W_{5}.(\\
\quad\mathrm{Cons}(W_{1},X,W_{2},Z),1(W_{1}),\\
\quad\mathrm{Cons}(W_{3},Z,W_{4},W_{2}),2(W_{3}),\\
\quad\mathrm{Cons}(W_{5},W_{2},Y,W_{4}),3(W_{5}),\\
\quad\mathrm{Nil}(W_{4},Y)\\
)\end{array}

The program for removing the last element from a doubly-linked list

)(W),\end{array}

(when it is given as a unary atom with the link
W
).
Alternatively, the function can be expressed in our formal notation
as

\displaystyle e_{\mathsf{DLpop}}\triangleq\begin{array}[]{l}(\lambda\,x[X,Y,Z].\\
\quad\mathbf{case}\;x[X,Y,Z]\;\mathbf{of}\\
\qquad\nu W_{1}W_{2}W_{3}.(\\
\qquad\quad y[W_{1},W_{2},X,Z],\\
\qquad\quad\mathrm{Cons}(W_{3},W_{2},Y,W_{1}),\\
\qquad\quad z[W_{3}],\\
\qquad\quad\mathrm{Nil}(W_{1},Y)\\
\qquad)\to\nu W.(y[Y,W,X,Z],\mathrm{Nil}(W,Y))\\
\quad\>\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to x[X,Y,Z]\\
)(W).\end{array}

As a function, only the node label (
\lambda
-abstraction) of the
atom matters, and the role of the
W
is to accommodate the function
inside a linked structure. If a function need not be put in a linked
structure, it can be represented as the label of a nullary atom, in
which case the
(W)
above is omitted
(as in
e_{\mathsf{LLT}}
defined later in (
2.1.1
)).

To illustrate the evaluation of this function, consider the doubly-linked list

G_{\mathsf{DL3}}
defined in (
2.1.1
).
Applying
e_{\mathsf{DLpop}}
to
G_{\mathsf{DL3}}
results in the following
two-step reduction (
Rd-
\beta
followed by
Rd-Case1
):

(23)

In this context,

\mathrm{N}
represents a node,
while
\mathrm{L}
represents a leaf.
To facilitate traversal, we introduce a distinguished leaf,
which is visually marked as

\mathrm{L}
.
This marked leaf serves as an indicator for traversal operations.

The program that applies a given function to the
value of a marked leaf of a leaf-linked tree
can be represented as follows:

Applying the function
e_{\mathsf{LLT}}
to a function
that returns a successor of a given number,
we obtain a function that produces a tree
in which the marked leaf contains the successor value,
and the marker is moved one step forward.
This is illustrated
as follows using the leaf-linked tree

t[L,R,X]
defined in (
2.1.1
).

(33)

Using a fixed point operator (i.e.,
let rec
),
we can define the map function that applies the given function
to all the leaves of the given leaf-linked tree.
Although
let rec
has been implemented
[
27
]
,
we focus on more non-obvious issues in the handling of graphs in

\lambda_{GT}
and leave its
the formal definition to an extended version of this paper.

2.2
Type System

The
\lambda_{GT}
language is equipped with a type system
that not only ensures type safety but also guarantees that operations over
data structures preserve their user-defined structural properties.
This section describes the type system first proposed in our
prior work
[
28
]

and examines its inherent limitations.

Our type system is formulated with four ingredients, (i) type names,
(ii) types (or type atoms), (iii) production rules, and (iv) typing
rules. We describe them step by step.

Firstly, we introduce
type names

\alpha,\beta,\dots
.
In concrete syntax, they are distinguished by using identifiers
starting with lowercase letters (as opposed to constructor names
starting with uppercase letters).

Secondly, we define the syntax of
type atoms
(or simply
types)

in
\lambda_{GT}
as follows:

Definition 2.6

(Types of
\lambda_{GT}
)
.

\tau\>\>::=\>\>(\tau\to\tau)(\overrightarrow{X})\mid\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})

∎

Thirdly, we introduce
production rules of hypergraphs

based on hypergraph grammar, which acts as a
counterpart of type definitions in standard functional languages.

Definition 2.7

(Production Rule)
.

\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})\longrightarrow\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{W\bowtie U},\overrightarrow{\tau})

For each production rule,
the set of the free links on the left- and the right-hand sides
must be equal, that is, we require that

\{\overrightarrow{X}\}=\bigl(\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\cup\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{W\bowtie U})\cup\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{\tau})\bigr)\setminus\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}.

Without loss of generality,
we also require that links in
\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{W\bowtie U})
are free
links of the right-hand side, i.e.,

\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{W\bowtie U})\cap\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}=\emptyset
.
This can be achieved by absorbing the fusions of local links
by preprocessing with structural congruence.
∎

Compared to the original definition
[
28
]
,
we have restricted the form of production rules to
what could be called a “standard form”to ensure
that each production rule has exactly one constructor atom on the
right-hand side.
This does not reduce the expressive power of the types,
as rules with multiple constructor atoms can be represented by
introducing auxiliary type names.

The types
(\tau\to\tau)(\overrightarrow{X})
and
\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})

correspond to arrow types and type
names in existing functional languages.
However, since the values, which are graphs, have free links in

\lambda_{GT}
,
the types also have free links.

Finally, we define
typing relation
and
typing rules
.

Definition 2.8

(Typing Environment)
.

A
typing environment

\Gamma
is
a set of bindings of the form
x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau
, where
we require that (i)
\{\overrightarrow{X}\}=\mathit{fn}(\tau)

to ensure the consistency of free links, and that (ii)
the links in
\overrightarrow{X}
are pairwise distinct.
We also require that the graph variables names occurring in a typing
environment are pairwise distinct.
∎

Definition 2.9

(Typing Relation)
.

A
typing relation
is represented as

\Gamma\vdash_{P}e:\tau,

where
\Gamma
is the typing environment,

P
is a set of production rules,

e
is an expression, and
\tau
is its type,
and

\mathit{fn}(e)=\mathit{fn}(\tau)
.
∎

A fundamental characteristic of the type system of
\lambda_{GT}

is that each type
\tau
contains zero or more free links,
which directly correspond to the free links present in the hypergraph values.

We introduce explicit type annotations to
\lambda
-abstractions

\lambda\,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau\,.\,e
.
In addition, we allow type annotations for graph variables occurring
within expressions.
In a case expression
(\mathbf{case}\;e_{1}\;\mathbf{of}\;T\to e_{2}\;\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to e_{3})
,
each graph variable occurring in
T
must occur with
a type annotation.
In the representation of the production rules,
rules with identical left-hand sides can be enumerated using
\mid
,
following the convention of formal grammars.

Definition 2.10

(Collecting Graph Variables with Type Annotations)
.

\displaystyle\mathit{vt}(\textbf{0})

\displaystyle\triangleq\emptyset

\displaystyle\mathit{vt}(p(\overrightarrow{X}))

\displaystyle\triangleq\emptyset

\displaystyle\mathit{vt}(x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau)

\displaystyle\triangleq\{x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau\}

\displaystyle\mathit{vt}((T_{1},T_{2}))

\displaystyle\triangleq\mathit{vt}(T_{1})\cup\mathit{vt}(T_{2})

\displaystyle\mathit{vt}(\nu X.T)

\displaystyle\triangleq\mathit{vt}(T)

∎

Definition 2.11

(Typing Rules)
.

The typing relation
\Gamma\vdash_{P}e:\tau

is deduced by the inference rules in
\figref
table:typing-rules.
∎

x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau\in\Gamma

Ty-Var

\Gamma\vdash_{P}x[\overrightarrow{Z}]:\tau\langle\overrightarrow{Z}/\overrightarrow{X}\rangle

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau_{1}\vdash_{P}e:\tau_{2}

Ty-Arrow

\Gamma\vdash_{P}(\lambda\,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau_{1}.e)(\overrightarrow{Z}):(\tau_{1}\to\tau_{2})(\overrightarrow{Z})

\Gamma\vdash_{P}e_{1}:(\tau_{1}\rightarrow\tau_{2})(\overrightarrow{Z})

\Gamma\vdash_{P}e_{2}:\tau_{1}

Ty-App

\Gamma\vdash_{P}(e_{1}\;e_{2}):\tau_{2}

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:\tau

Y\notin\mathit{fn}(T)

Ty-Alpha

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T\langle Y/X\rangle:\tau\langle Y/X\rangle

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:\tau

T\equiv T^{\prime}

Ty-Cong

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T^{\prime}:\tau

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T_{1}:\tau_{1}

\dots

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T_{n}:\tau_{n}

Ty-Prod

\Gamma\mathrel{\vdash_{P}}\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V},T_{1},\dots,T_{n}):\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})

where

(\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})\longrightarrow\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V},\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{n}))\in P

\Gamma\vdash_{P}e_{1}:\tau_{1}

\Gamma,\mathit{vt}(T)\vdash_{P}e_{2}:\tau_{2}

\Gamma\vdash_{P}e_{3}:\tau_{2}

Ty-Case

\Gamma\vdash_{P}(\mathbf{case}\;e_{1}\;\mathbf{of}\;T\to e_{2}\;\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to e_{3}):\tau_{2}

Figure 6:
Typing Rules of
\lambda_{GT}
.

Ty-Var
,
Ty-Arrow
, and
Ty-App
,
are analogous to those of conventional functional type systems
except that the free links of variables must be properly handled.
In contrast,

Ty-Alpha
,
Ty-Cong
, and
Ty-Prod
are specific
to the hypergraph incorporation of
\lambda_{GT}
.

Ty-Cong
incorporates structural congruence
into the reduction relation.

Ty-Alpha

\alpha
-converts the free link names of both the graph and
its type.

Ty-Prod
incorporates production rules to the type system.
Each
\tau_{i}
denotes a type atom occurring in the right-hand
side
of a production rule, and each
T_{i}
denotes an expression
of type
\tau_{i}
.
By simultaneously replacing each
\tau_{i}

by the corresponding
T_{i}
,
the right-hand side of the production rule
is transformed into an expression of type
\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})
.

Ty-Case
defines the typing rule for the case expression.

The type system proposed in prior research
[
28
]
was not fully static;
instead, it relied on dynamic checking for case expressions.

Definition 2.12

(Dynamic Type Checking in Case Expressions)
.

The reduction relation of case expressions with dynamic checking is defined in

\figref
fig:refined-rd-case.
∎

In dynamic type checking for case expressions,
after pattern matching has been performed,
the runtime system checks whether there exists a graph substitution
\overrightarrow{\theta}

that satisfies
G\equiv T\overrightarrow{\theta}
,
and checks that all type annotations
for the graph variables within
T
are satisfied.
Here,
P
denotes the set of production rules
used to type the case expression.
If the matching with the type constraints succeeds,
evaluation proceeds along

Rd-Case1
;
otherwise,
evaluation follows
Rd-Case2
.

The fundamental reason why static type checking is difficult in pattern matching
stems from the structural complexity of the underlying computational model.
Unlike conventional functional programming languages that operate on tree-like data structures,
the language under consideration employs graph-based structures.
Graphs inherently exhibit a higher degree of complexity compared to trees,
introducing significant challenges in enforcing static type constraints.
Furthermore, as demonstrated earlier,
the expressiveness of the pattern matching mechanism in this language surpasses
that of conventional algebraic data type (ADT) pattern matching.
For instance, it permits direct matching on the tail of a list and the leaves of a leaf-linked tree,
which extends beyond the capabilities typically supported in ADT-based pattern matching.
This enhanced expressiveness introduces additional difficulties in establishing a
fully-static type system.

\begin{array}[]{c}G\equiv T\overrightarrow{\theta}\land\bigwedge_{x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau\in\mathit{vt}(T)}\bigl(\emptyset\vdash_{P}x[\overrightarrow{X}]\overrightarrow{\theta}:\tau\bigr)\end{array}

Rd-Case1

E[\mathbf{case}\;G\;\mathbf{of}\;T\to e_{1}\;\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to e_{2}]\>\longrightarrow_{\mathit{val}}\>E[e_{1}\overrightarrow{\theta}]

\not\exists\overrightarrow{\theta}.\bigl(G\equiv T\overrightarrow{\theta}\land\bigwedge_{x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau\in\mathit{vt}(T)}\bigl(\emptyset\vdash_{P}x[\overrightarrow{X}]\overrightarrow{\theta}:\tau\bigr)\bigr)

Rd-Case2

E[\mathbf{case}\;G\;\mathbf{of}\;T\to e_{1}\;\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to e_{2}]\>\longrightarrow_{\mathit{val}}\>E[e_{2}]

Figure 7:
Refined Reduction Relation for Case Expressions.

2.2.1
Motivating Examples

The type system of
\lambda_{GT}

allows users to define custom shapes such as
doubly-linked lists and leaf-linked trees.

For instance, the production rules for doubly-linked lists
and leaf-linked trees are

Formally, the production rules can be expressed
as follows.

\displaystyle P_{\textsf{DL-LLT}}\triangleq\left\{\begin{array}[]{@{}lll}\mathit{dbllist}(X,Y,Z)\longrightarrow\\
\quad\;\;\mathrm{Nil}(X,Z),Y\bowtie Z\\[2.84526pt]
\quad\mid\nu W_{1}W_{2}.(\mathrm{Cons}(W_{1},X,W_{2},Z),\\
\qquad\mathit{nat}(W_{1}),\mathit{dbllist}(Z,Y,W_{2}))\\[8.53581pt]
\mathit{nat}(X)\longrightarrow 1(X)\mid 2(X)\mid\dots\\[8.53581pt]
\mathit{lltree}(L,R,X)\longrightarrow\\
\quad\;\;\nu W_{1}.(\mathrm{Leaf}(W_{1},R,X),L\bowtie X,\mathit{nat}(W_{1}))\\[2.84526pt]
\quad\mid\nu W_{1}.(\mathrm{LeafM}(W_{1},R,X),L\bowtie X,\mathit{nat}(W_{1}))\\[2.84526pt]
\quad\mid\nu YW_{1}W_{2}.(\mathrm{Node}(W_{1},W_{2},X),\\
\qquad\mathit{lltree}(L,Y,W_{1}),\mathit{lltree}(Y,R,W_{1}))\\
\end{array}\right.

Ty-Alpha
,
Ty-Cong
, and
Ty-Prod
,
the following typing relations can be derived.

2.3
Open Challenges

As described above,
although the type system of
\lambda_{GT}
is highly promising
and capable of handling many practical examples,
several open challenges remain.

One key challenge is
typing partially constructed graphs,
such as doubly-linked lists without tails or leaf-linked trees that lack certain leaves,
as outlined in Requirement 6
in the beginning of
Section

2
.
The previous work partially addressed
this problem by requiring users to define types for such incomplete graphs (e.g., difference lists)
separately from the types of fully constructed graphs
[
28
]
.
However, this approach is cumbersome
and does not generalise well to more complex cases,
in which structural incompleteness is more intricate and difficult to express within the type system.

Another key challenge is achieving
a fully static type system,
as outlined in
Requirement 7.
The type system proposed in
[
28
]
is mostly static, but
during pattern matching,
it still relies on dynamic type checking.

To overcome these challenges,
we propose an extension to the type system incorporating linear implication types,
which enables typing of incomplete structures (Requirement 6),
while eliminating the reliance on dynamic type checking (Requirement 7).

3
Introducing Linear Implication Types

\lambda_{GT}
enables declarative programming based on
graph pattern matching and graph composition,
supported by a type system that ensures their shapes.

However, its existing type system lacks static typing of incomplete
data structures.
To address this limitation,
we propose an extended type system that introduces

linear implication types
(
\multimap
) and proves its
soundness (with dynamic type checking in case expressions).

The rest of this section proceeds in the following steps.

Section

3.1
introduces linear implication types and the type
system extended by linear implication types.

Section

3.2
discusses the (non-obvious) design of linear
implication types.

Section

3.3
presents some typing examples with
complete proof trees.

Section

3.4
discusses the properties of the typing
rules. In particular, we show that the rule
Ty-Prod
becomes admissible
by newly introduced typing rules.

Section

3.5
discusses the soundness of the type system.

3.1
The Extended Type System

We extend the type system of
\lambda_{GT}

by incorporating the
linear implication type

(\{\overrightarrow{\tau}\}\multimap\tau)\{\overrightarrow{X}\}

into the type system.
By abuse of notation, we write the linear implication type
simply as
(\overrightarrow{\tau}\multimap\tau){\{\overrightarrow{X}\}}
and assume that
the
\overrightarrow{\tau}
on the left operand of
\multimap
is a multiset
that allows us to reorder its elements whenever necessary.
Let
\emptyset
stand for an empty
\overrightarrow{\tau}
.
The necessity of explicitly specifying the set of free links
\{\overrightarrow{X}\}

will be discussed later in
Section

3.2
.

As will be explained shortly, we adopt this form of linear implication
(as opposed to a standard form and currying

\tau_{1}\multimap\tau_{2}\multimap\dots\multimap\tau_{n}
)
to smoothly relate it to production rules.

We refine the type in
Definition

2.6
as follows.

Definition 3.1

(Syntax of the Type, Revised)
.

\tau::=(\overrightarrow{\tau}\multimap\tau){\{\overrightarrow{X}\}}\mid(\tau\to\tau)(\overrightarrow{X})\mid\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})

∎

In order to keep the theory not too complicated, henceforth we assume that
the above extension does not apply to types used in the following contexts
(though we believe that this restriction is not essential):

1.

types occurring in the left- and right-hand sides of
\multimap
and
\to

are
\multimap
-free,

2.

types occurring in the right-hand sides of production rules
(
Definition

2.7
) are
\multimap
-free, and

3.

the first subexpression of a
case
expression cannot be
of a linear implication type.

The above three restrictions are essentially
to avoid the generation and handling
of curried forms of
\multimap
which we are
going to dispense with (as explained above) in proofs etc.

The linear implication type
(\overrightarrow{\tau_{1}}\multimap\tau_{2}){\{\overrightarrow{X}\}}

represents a structure with free links
\overrightarrow{X}
,
which attains the type
\tau_{2}
when any (sub)graphs of types

\overrightarrow{\tau_{1}}
is supplied.
This differs fundamentally from arrow types
(\tau_{1}\to\tau_{2})(\overrightarrow{X})
.
Arrow types are
types for functions (
\lambda
-abstractions),
which define transformations over expressions rather than data structures.
On the other hand, linear implication types are types for direct transformations over
data structures.

The incorporation of this type is motivated by the
Magic Wand

operator in Separation Logic
[
18
]

and the
Difference Type
in LMNtalGG
[
33
]
.
This extension provides a formal mechanism for explicitly managing
the type of incomplete structures.

We provide an intuitive explanation of how linear implication
enables the typing of data structures with missing elements.

(58)

This represents that the graph variable
y[W_{1},W_{2},X,Z]

matches a subgraph that is an incomplete graph
that will become a doubly-linked list
if we supply a doubly-linked list at the end.

Formally, the graph variable
y
can be type-annotated as

\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{lll}y[W_{1},W_{2},X,Z]:\\
\quad(\mathit{dbllist}(W_{2},Y,W_{1})\multimap\\
\qquad\mathit{dbllist}(X,Y,Z)){\{W_{1},W_{2},X,Z\}}.\end{array}

We define the free links of the linear implication type

(\overrightarrow{\tau}\multimap\tau){\{\overrightarrow{X}\}}
as

\mathit{fn}((\overrightarrow{\tau}_{1}\multimap\tau_{2}){\{\overrightarrow{X}\}})\triangleq\{\overrightarrow{X}\}.

We discuss in
Section

3.2

why linear implication types require the explicit notation
\overrightarrow{X}
of
free links.

Although the linear implication type
(\overrightarrow{\tau}\multimap\tau){\{\overrightarrow{X}\}}

and the function type
(\overrightarrow{\tau}\to\tau)(\overrightarrow{X})
look syntactically similar,
they serve fundamentally different roles:
Unlike the function type
(\overrightarrow{\tau}\to\tau)(\overrightarrow{X})
,
which represent the type of functions that contain expressions,
the linear implication type
(\overrightarrow{\tau}\multimap\tau){\{\overrightarrow{X}\}}

is for operations on data structures based on
the decomposition and composition of subgraphs.

For defining the typing rules for the linear implication type later,
we define link substitution for linear implication types as follows.

Definition 3.2

(Link Substitution, Extended)
.

Given a substitution
\sigma
,
the substitution of a linear implication type is defined as

\begin{array}[]{lll}((\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{n}\multimap\tau){\{X_{1},\dots,X_{n}\}})\sigma\triangleq\\
\quad(\tau_{1}\sigma,\dots,\tau_{n}\sigma\multimap\tau\sigma){\{X_{1}\sigma,\dots,X_{n}\sigma\}}.\end{array}

∎

We then present the newly added typing rules.

Definition 3.3

(Newly Added Typing Rules)
.

The newly added typing rules that incorporate linear implication types
are defined in
\figref
table:revised-typing-rules.
∎

Ty-LI-Intro

\Gamma\vdash_{P}(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{W\bowtie U}):(\overrightarrow{\tau}\multimap\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})){\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}}

where

(\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})\longrightarrow\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{W\bowtie U},\overrightarrow{\tau}))\in P\text{ and }\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}=\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\cup\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{W\bowtie U}).\hskip 120.0pt

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T_{1}:(\tau_{2},\overrightarrow{\tau_{1}}\multimap\tau_{1}){\{\overrightarrow{X}\}}

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T_{2}:(\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}}\multimap\tau_{2}){\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}}

Ty-LI-Trans

\Gamma\vdash_{P}\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(T_{1},T_{2}):(\overrightarrow{\tau_{1}},\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}}\multimap\tau_{1}){\{\overrightarrow{W}\}}

where
\begin{array}[t]{cl@{\qquad}clll}(i)&\{\overrightarrow{X},\overrightarrow{Y}\}\setminus\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}=\{\overrightarrow{W}\}&(ii)&\{\overrightarrow{X}\}\cap\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{2})\\
(iii)&\{\overrightarrow{X}\}\cap\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{2})&(iv)&\bigl(\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\cup\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}})\bigr)\cap\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{\tau_{1}})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{2})\\
(v)&\mathit{fn}(\tau_{1})\subseteq\{\overrightarrow{W}\}\cup\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{\tau_{1}},\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}})\end{array}

Here,
\overrightarrow{\tau_{i}}
denotes
\tau_{i1},\dots,\tau_{in}

and is different from
\tau_{i}
.

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:(\emptyset\multimap\tau){\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}}

Ty-LI-Elim0

\Gamma\vdash_{P}\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.T:\tau

where
\mathit{fn}(T)=\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}

and
\mathit{fn}(T)\setminus\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}=\mathit{fn}(\tau)
.

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:\tau

Ty-LI-Intro0

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:(\emptyset\multimap\tau){\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}}

where
\mathit{fn}(T)=\mathit{fn}(\tau)=\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}
.

Figure 8:
Newly Added Typing Rules.

Let us explain the individual rules.

Ty-LI-Intro
is intuitively read as: “a graph (atom)
C(\overrightarrow{Y})
has
the type which states that
C(\overrightarrow{Y})
is obtained from a graph of type

\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})
by removing graphs of types
\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{n}
.”

Ty-LI-Intro
is designed in this form to smoothly relate production
rules and the linear implication type. Indeed, the form of the linear
implication type that allows a multiset of types as its antecedent is
exactly motivated by this relation.

Ty-LI-Trans
states the transitivity of linear implication;
it states that two linear implications can be fused by cancelling
\tau_{2}
.
The free link condition (i) comes from the constraint that free links of
the subject and its type must have the same set of free links.
The remaining conditions (ii)–(v) are technical side constraints
whose detailed roles are explained in Appendix
C
,
where we also clarify how and where each condition is employed.

Ty-LI-Trans
is thought of a generalisation of the standard elimination
rule of linear implication.

These introduction and elimination rules are accompanied by two ‘base
cases’, namely
Ty-LI-Elim0
and
Ty-LI-Intro0
, for handling linear
implication with empty antecedents.

The standard elimination rule of linear implication
could be represented as follows.

Definition 3.4

(Elimination of Linear Implication)
.

\begin{array}[]{c}\Gamma\vdash_{P}y[\overrightarrow{Y}]:(\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{n}\multimap\tau){\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}}\\
\Gamma\vdash_{P}T_{1}:\tau_{1}\quad\dots\quad\Gamma\vdash_{P}T_{n}:\tau_{n}\end{array}

Ty-LI-E

\Gamma\vdash_{P}\nu\overrightarrow{X}.(y[\overrightarrow{Y}],T_{1},\dots,T_{n}):\tau

where
\mathit{fn}(\nu\overrightarrow{X}.(y[\overrightarrow{Y}],T_{1},\dots,T_{n}))=\mathit{fn}(\tau)
.
∎

We note that this rule
is admissible and can be derived easily using
Ty-LI-Trans
,

Ty-LI-Elim0
, and
Ty-LI-Intro0
.
The constraint on free links,

\mathit{fn}(\nu\overrightarrow{X}.(y[\overrightarrow{Y}],T_{1},\dots,T_{n}))=\mathit{fn}(\tau)
,
is derived from the
free link conditions of
Ty-LI-Trans
,
Ty-LI-Elim0
, and
Ty-LI-Intro0
.

3.2
Free Links of Linear Implication Types

In this section, we examine the need of the explicit notation of free
links
(\overrightarrow{X})
in linear
implication types
(\tau_{1}\multimap\tau_{2}){\{\overrightarrow{X}\}}
.

At first glance, it might appear that the free link set of a linear
implication type
\overrightarrow{X}

could be defined based on the free link sets of its antecedent and
consequent types.

For example, consider the type annotation (
3.1
).
The free links of the expression
y[W_{1},W_{2},X,Z]
is

\{W_{1},W_{2},X,Z\}
.
One may think that this is obtained as the symmetric difference of the
sets of free links of the two operands, i.e.,

(\{W_{2},Y,W_{1}\}\setminus\{X,Y,Z\})\cup(\{X,Y,Z\}\setminus\{W_{2},Y,W_{1}\}
,
which gives
\{W_{1},W_{2},X,Z\}
in this particular example.
However, it is not obvious whether this idea generalises to all
cases.

To illustrate this point, let
T_{0}
be a graph (or
a graph variable) such that

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T_{0}:(\tau_{1}\multimap\tau_{2}){\{\overrightarrow{X}\}}
for some

\Gamma
and
P
.
That is,
T_{0}
represents a graph that will acquire type

\tau_{2}
upon supplying a graph of type
\tau_{1}
.
Let
T_{1}
be a graph of type
\tau_{1}
,
and
T_{2}
be a graph
\nu\overrightarrow{X}.(T_{0},T_{1})

satisfying
\mathit{fn}(\nu\overrightarrow{X}.(T_{0},T_{1}))=\mathit{fn}(T_{2})
,
which, by the definition of
T_{0}
, is given the type
\tau_{2}
.

The free link sets of the expressions
T_{0}
,
T_{1}
, and

T_{2}\triangleq\nu\overrightarrow{X}.(T_{0},T_{1})

an be classified as in

\tabref
table:revision-comparison,
with each category labelled from 1 to 8.
Note that the free links
\overrightarrow{X}_{8}
do not occur anywhere and that
the free links
\overrightarrow{X}_{7}
are not possible by definition.
The remaining six categories are visualised in

\figref
fig:li-freelinks-vis.

Table 1:
Free Links of Graphs Enumerated.

Figure 9:
Free Links of Graphs Visualised.

Among the free links,
\overrightarrow{X}_{2}
,

\overrightarrow{X}_{4}
and
\overrightarrow{X}_{6}
may be ignored as they
are absorbed by
\nu\overrightarrow{X}
.
It remains crucial to distinguish between
\overrightarrow{X}_{1}
and
\overrightarrow{X}_{5}
, where

\overrightarrow{X}_{1}
belongs to
\mathit{fn}(T_{0})
, whereas
\overrightarrow{X}_{5}
does not.
However, using only the free link sets of
T_{1}
and
T_{2}
,
it is not possible to differentiate between
\overrightarrow{X}_{1}
and
\overrightarrow{X}_{5}
.
Consequently, even when
\mathit{fn}(\tau_{1})=\mathit{fn}(T_{1})
and
\mathit{fn}(\tau_{2})=\mathit{fn}(T_{2})
hold,
the free link set of
T_{0}:\tau_{1}\multimap\tau_{2}

cannot be determined solely from
\tau_{1}
and
\tau_{2}
.
To resolve this issue,
an explicit annotation of the free link set
\overrightarrow{X}\triangleq\mathit{fn}(T_{0})

is incorporated into the type, denoted as
(\tau_{1}\multimap\tau_{2}){\{\overrightarrow{X}\}}
.

The above observation is in contrast with
a typing framework of LMNtal (without hyperlinks)
that incorporates the notion of
difference types

[
33
]

that can be thought of as a counterpart of to our linear implication
types for incomplete hypergraphs.
In
[
33
]
, such explicit annotation is unnecessary
because the language enforces a structural constraint
whereby a link occurring exactly twice within a term is classified as
a local link, which means that any link that is a free link in both

T_{0}
and
T_{1}
must necessarily be a local link in
T_{2}
.
This property allows the set of free links in
T_{0}

to be derived solely from the free link sets of
T_{1}
and
T_{2}

as their symmetric difference.

3.3
Typing Examples

In this section, we present an application of the linear implication type.
We first show the typing of a segment of a doubly-linked list,
and then a program that removes the last element of a doubly-linked list.

3.3.1
Doubly-Linked List Segments

First we revisit the production rules for doubly-linked lists in

P_{\textsf{DL-LLT}}
(
2.2.1
) (
Section

2.2.1
):

\displaystyle\begin{array}[]{@{}lll}\mathit{dbllist}(X,Y,Z)\longrightarrow\mathrm{Nil}(X,Z),Y\bowtie Z\\[2.84526pt]
\quad\mid\nu W_{1}W_{2}.(\mathrm{Cons}(W_{1},X,W_{2},Z),\\
\qquad\mathit{nat}(W_{1}),\mathit{dbllist}(Z,Y,W_{2})).\end{array}

Now we consider the typing of a fragment of a doubly-linked list that consists of two adjacent
\mathrm{Cons}{}
nodes with
\mathit{nat}
elements:

\begin{array}[]{l}\nu W_{1}.(\mathrm{Cons}(W_{1},X,W_{2},Z),3(W_{1})),\\
\quad\nu W_{3}.(\mathrm{Cons}(W_{3},Z,W_{4},W_{2}),5(W_{3})).\end{array}

(65)

This graph is of type

(\mathit{dbllist}(W_{2},Y,W_{4})\multimap\mathit{dbllist}(X,Y,Z)){\{W_{4},W_{2},X,Z\}}

as shown in
Figure

10
.

\psi(1)\triangleq

Ty-LI-Intro

\begin{array}[b]{llll}\vdash_{P_{\textsf{DL-LLT}}}\mathrm{Cons}(W_{1},X,W_{2},Z)\\
:(\mathit{nat}(W_{1}),\mathit{dbllist}(Z,Y,W_{2})\multimap\mathit{dbllist}(X,Y,Z)){\{W_{1},X,W_{2},Z\}}\end{array}

\vdash_{P_{\textsf{DL-LLT}}}3(W_{1}):(\emptyset\multimap\mathit{nat}(W_{1})){\{W_{1}\}}

Ty-LI-Trans

\vdash_{P_{\textsf{DL-LLT}}}\nu W_{1}.(\mathrm{Cons}(W_{1},X,W_{2},Z),3(W_{1})):(\mathit{dbllist}(Z,Y,W_{2})\multimap\mathit{dbllist}(X,Y,Z)){\{X,W_{2},Z\}}

\psi(1)

3.3.2
Pattern Matching at the List Tail

In this section, we present an application of the linear implication type
by assigning types to a program that removes the last element of a doubly-linked list.

First, consider the expression
e_{\mathsf{DLpop}}

(
2.1.1
) (
Section

2.1.1
).
In this case, we refine the case expression template
by explicitly adding type annotations to the graph variable
y
and
z
,
illustrated as follows:

\displaystyle e_{\mathsf{DLpop}}^{\prime}\triangleq\begin{array}[]{l}(\lambda\,x[X,Y,Z]:\mathit{dbllist}(X,Y,Z).\\
\quad\mathbf{case}\;x[X,Y,Z]\;\mathbf{of}\\
\qquad\nu W_{1}W_{2}W_{3}.(\\
\quad\qquad y[W_{1},W_{2},X,Z]:\\
\qquad\qquad(\mathit{dbllist}(W_{2},Y,W_{1})\multimap\\
\qquad\qquad\quad\mathit{dbllist}(X,Y,Z)){\{W_{1},W_{2},X,Z\}},\\
\quad\qquad\mathrm{Cons}(W_{3},W_{2},Y,W_{1}),\\
\quad\qquad z[W_{3}]:\mathit{nat}(W_{3}),\\
\quad\qquad\mathrm{Nil}(W_{1},Y)\\
\qquad)\to\nu W.(y[Y,W,X,Z],\mathrm{Nil}(W,Y))\\
\quad\>\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to x[X,Y,Z]\\
)(W).\end{array}

We now demonstrate that, given
P_{\textsf{DL-LLT}}
(
2.2.1
)
and
e_{\mathsf{DLpop}}^{\prime}
(
3.3.2
),
we can derive the typing judgement:

\displaystyle\emptyset\vdash_{P_{\textsf{DL-LLT}}}e_{\mathsf{DLpop}}^{\prime}:(\mathit{dbllist}(X,Y,Z)\to\mathit{dbllist}(X,Y,Z))(W).

(79)

The detailed derivation of this typing judgement is illustrated
in
\figref
fig:dbllist-removal-typing-derivation-eg.

For
e_{\mathsf{DLpop}}^{\prime}

(
3.3.2

3.5
Soundness of the Type System with Linear Implication Types

This section proves the type preservation and progress properties
of
\lambda_{GT}
’s type system with linear implication types.

For brevity, we omit the set
P
of production rules from typing
relations
\vdash_{P}
and just write
\vdash
.
Also, for simplicity, we assume that every graph variable name has
its own arity;
i.e., we disallow any graph variable name to occur with different
arities (and stand for different variables).

Lemma 3.5

(Weakening)
.

If
\Gamma\vdash e:\tau
and

x[\overrightarrow{X}]\not\in\mathrm{dom}(\Gamma)
, then

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash e:\tau
.

Proof.

By induction on the derivation tree of the typing relation

\Gamma\vdash e:\tau
.
For a derivation tree consisting of a single
Ty-Var
, augmenting
the environment with a fresh binding does not invalidate the
derivation. For all other derivation trees, the final step of the
derivation (with a rule other than
Ty-Var
) does not depend on the
content of the environment
\Gamma
, which can therefore be augmented.
∎

The following Substitution Lemma plays the key role in establishing
the preservation property.

Lemma 3.6

(Substitution Lemma)
.

If
\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash e:\tau
and

\Gamma\vdash G:\tau^{\prime}
, then

\Gamma\vdash e[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau
.

The proof technique is standard, i.e.,
by induction on the derivation tree of the typing relation and case
analysis by the typing rule used in the final step, but
the handling of two kinds of substitution (graph substitution and
link substitution), structural congruence, and so on, needs special care.
We postpone its complete proof to Appendix
B
.

Before proving the preservation properties, we
we show type preservation of evaluation contexts.

Lemma 3.7

(Evaluation Context Preservation)
.

If

\Gamma\vdash E[e]:\tau
, there exists
\tau^{\prime}
such that

\Gamma\vdash e:\tau^{\prime}
, and for all
e^{\prime}
such that

\Gamma\vdash e^{\prime}:\tau^{\prime}
,
\Gamma\vdash E[e^{\prime}]:\tau
holds.

Proof.

Based on straightforward induction
on the form of evaluation contexts

E[e]
.
If
E=[\,]
, the claim holds trivially.
Otherwise, i.e., if

E[e]
is
\textbf{case}\ E^{\prime}[e]\ \textbf{of}\ \dots
or

(E^{\prime}[e]\,e_{2})
or
(G\,E^{\prime}[e])
,

E^{\prime}[e]
and
E^{\prime}[e^{\prime}]
have the same type by the induction hypothesis, and
the final step of the derivation tree with
Ty-Case
or
Ty-App

establishes
\Gamma\vdash E[e^{\prime}]:\tau
.
∎

Theorem 3.8

(Preservation / Subject Reduction)
.

If
\Gamma\vdash e:\tau
and
e\>\longrightarrow_{\mathit{val}}\>e^{\prime}
, then

\Gamma\vdash e^{\prime}:\tau
.

Proof.

By
Figure

5
, without loss of generality,
we can assume that
e
is of the form

E[e_{0}]
, where (i)
E
is an evaluation context and
(ii)
e_{0}
is
a redex such that
e_{0}\>\longrightarrow_{\mathit{val}}\>e_{0}^{\prime}
for some
e_{0}^{\prime}
,
which implies
E[e_{0}]\>\longrightarrow_{\mathit{val}}\>E[e_{0}^{\prime}]
.
We prove

\Gamma\vdash e_{0}:\tau_{0}\implies\Gamma\vdash e_{0}^{\prime}:\tau_{0}

by case analysis on the rule used for reduction:

Rd-
\beta
,
Rd-Case1
, or
Rd-Case2
.

Case
Rd-
\boldsymbol{\beta}
:
The reduction is of the following form.

\mathit{fn}(G)=\{\overrightarrow{X}\}

Rd-
\beta

((\lambda\,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau_{1}.\,e_{1})(\overrightarrow{Y})\>G)\>\longrightarrow_{\mathit{val}}\>e_{1}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]

Since an application can be typed only with
Ty-App
,
the typing of the subject
e_{0}
must use
Ty-App
, whose premises are

•

\Gamma\vdash(\lambda x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau_{1}.\,e_{1})(\overrightarrow{Y}):(\tau_{1}\to\tau_{0})(\overrightarrow{Y})

and

•

\Gamma\vdash G:\tau_{1}
.

The derivation of

\Gamma\vdash(\lambda x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau_{1}.\,e_{1})(\overrightarrow{Y}):(\tau_{1}\to\tau)(\overrightarrow{Y})

must use
Ty-Arrow
, whose premise is

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau_{1}\vdash e_{1}:\tau_{0}
.
With this and the substitution lemma, we have

\Gamma\vdash e_{1}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau_{0}.

Case
Rd-Case1
:

The reduction is of the form

G\equiv T\overrightarrow{\theta}\land\bigwedge_{i}\bigl(\emptyset\vdash x_{i}[\overrightarrow{X}_{i}]\overrightarrow{\theta}:\sigma_{i}\bigr)

Rd-Case1

(\mathbf{case}\;G\;\mathbf{of}\;T\to e_{1}\;\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to e_{2})\>\longrightarrow_{\mathit{val}}\>e_{1}\overrightarrow{\theta}

where

\overrightarrow{\theta}\mathord{=}[G_{1}/x_{1}[\overrightarrow{X}_{1}]]\dots[G_{n}/x_{n}[\overrightarrow{X}_{n}]]

such that
\{x_{1}[\overrightarrow{X}_{1}],

\dots,x_{n}[\overrightarrow{X}_{n}]\}
is the set of graph
variables in
T
.
The typing of this case expression can be done only with
Ty-Case
:

\Gamma\vdash G:\tau^{\prime}

(\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime})\vdash e_{1}:\tau_{0}

\Gamma\vdash e_{2}:\tau_{0}

Ty-Case

\Gamma\vdash(\mathbf{case}\;G\;\mathbf{of}\;T\to e_{1}\;\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to e_{2}):\tau_{0}

where each graph variable occurring
in
T
must occur with a type annotation

x_{i}[\overrightarrow{X_{i}}]:\sigma_{i}
,
and

\Gamma^{\prime}=x_{1}[\overrightarrow{X}_{1}]:\sigma_{1},\dots,x_{n}[\overrightarrow{X}_{n}]:\sigma_{n}
.
By applying the substitution lemma
n
times, from the second premise

\Gamma,x_{1}[\overrightarrow{X}_{1}]:\sigma_{1},\dots,x_{n}[\overrightarrow{X}_{n}]:\sigma_{n}\vdash e_{1}:\tau_{0},

we can get

\Gamma\vdash e_{1}[G_{1}/x_{1}[\overrightarrow{X}_{1}]]\dots[G_{n}/x_{n}[\overrightarrow{X}_{n}]]:\tau_{0}

provided that we have
n
typing relations

\Gamma\vdash G_{1}:\sigma_{1},\dots,\Gamma\vdash G_{n}:\sigma_{n}.

These
n
typing relations can be obtained
by applying the weakening lemma to the family of premises of
Rd-Case1

because
G_{i}=x_{i}[\overrightarrow{X}_{i}]\overrightarrow{\theta}
.
Thus we have derived

\Gamma\vdash e_{1}\overrightarrow{\theta}:\tau_{0}
.

Case
Rd-Case2
:

The typing of the case expression must use
Ty-Case
above, which contains

\Gamma\vdash e_{2}:\tau_{0}
; therefore we have

\Gamma\vdash e_{0}^{\prime}:\tau_{0}
.

To summarise, let
e=E[e_{0}]
.
If
e_{0}\>\longrightarrow_{\mathit{val}}\>e_{0}^{\prime}
and
\Gamma\vdash e_{0}:\tau_{0}
,
then we have
\Gamma\vdash e_{0}^{\prime}:\tau_{0}
and

\Gamma\vdash E[e_{0}^{\prime}]:\tau
from
Lemma

3.7
.
Therefore,

\Gamma\vdash e:\tau\ \land\ e\>\longrightarrow_{\mathit{val}}\>e^{\prime}\implies\Gamma\vdash e^{\prime}:\tau

and the claim is established.
∎

Theorem 3.9

(Progress)
.

If
\emptyset\vdash e:\tau
, then either
e
is a value or there
exists
e^{\prime}
such that
e\>\longrightarrow_{\mathit{val}}\>e^{\prime}
.

Proof.

By induction on the structure of the expression
e
.

If
e
is a template
T
, the assumption that the typing
environment is empty implies that
T
contains no type variable
and hence is a value.

If
e
is a case expression, by the induction hypothesis
either the evaluation of the condition
makes progress, or the condition is a value and the
case expression
is reduced to one of the two branches.

If
e
is an application
(e_{1}\,e_{2})
and

e_{1}
is a value,
e_{1}
must be a
\lambda
-atom because
e
is
well-typed.
If
e_{2}
is a value as well,
then
(e_{1}\,e_{2})
is a
\beta
-redex;
otherwise, by the induction hypothesis

e_{2}\>\longrightarrow_{\mathit{val}}\>e_{2}^{\prime}
and hence

(e_{1}\,e_{2})\>\longrightarrow_{\mathit{val}}\>\ (e_{1}\,e_{2}^{\prime})
.
If
e_{1}
is not a value, by the induction hypothesis

e_{1}\>\longrightarrow_{\mathit{val}}\>e_{1}^{\prime}
and hence
e\>\longrightarrow_{\mathit{val}}\>(e_{1}^{\prime}\,e_{2})
.
∎

Corollary 3.10

(Type Soundness)
.

If
\emptyset\vdash e:\tau
and

e\>\longrightarrow_{\mathtt{val}}^{*}\>e^{\prime}
with

e^{\prime}
normal (no further steps), then
e^{\prime}
is a value of type

\tau
.

Proof.

Follows from repeated application of

Theorem

3.8
and

Theorem

3.9
.
∎

4
Fully-Static Type System

In the previous type systems (Sections
2
and
3
),
the typing rule
Ty-Case
for
case
expressions
does not impose any special constraints on the type
\tau_{1}
of the expression
e_{1}
.
Even when
\tau_{1}
does not match the type expected by the pattern,
the evaluation remains sound under dynamic checks:
if the match fails, the evaluation proceeds to the
otherwise
branch,
and if the match succeeds, the necessary checks are performed dynamically.

However, when dynamic checks at runtime are eliminated,
soundness can no longer be preserved by simply using the
Ty-Case
rule as it is.
To address this, in this section we introduce additional constraints
that guarantee soundness of a fully static type system
without relying on the dynamic checks originally embedded in
case
expressions.

First, in
Section

4.1
,
we modify the
Ty-Case
rule so that
the consistency between the type expected by the pattern and the type
of the scrutinee (graph under scrutiny)
can be checked statically.
However, this modification alone is not sufficient:
as shown in
\figref
fig:unsound-dbllist-removal-typederiv-eg,
a counterexample still exists.
Therefore, to resolve the unsoundness that remains even after modifying the rule,
we introduce additional constraints.

In
Section

4.2
, we give a formal definition of these constraints.

Finally, in
Section

4.3
,
we provide a proof sketch of soundness for the extended type system
that incorporates these modifications and constraints.

4.1
Observation

First, we modify the
Ty-Case
rule
so that the consistency between the type expected by the pattern
and the type of the matching expression in a
case
expression
can be checked statically.
We then explain why this modification alone causes problems
when dynamic checking is omitted.
Finally, we discuss the additional constraints
introduced to resolve this issue.

We introduce the revised typing rule for
case
expressions,
shown in
Definition

4.1
.

Definition 4.1

(Revised
Ty-Case
)
.

\begin{array}[]{c}\Gamma\vdash_{P}e_{1}:\tau_{1}\\
\Gamma,\mathit{vt}(T)\vdash_{P}e_{2}:\tau_{2}\end{array}

\begin{array}[]{c}\mathit{vt}(T)\vdash_{P}T:\tau_{1}\\
\Gamma\vdash_{P}e_{3}:\tau_{2}\end{array}

Ty-Case

\Gamma\vdash_{P}(\mathbf{case}\;e_{1}\;\mathbf{of}\;T\to e_{2}\;\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to e_{3}):\tau_{2}

∎

Ty-Case
is the revised typing rule for case expressions.
This rule defines the type assignment for conditional expressions
that perform structural analysis on graph-based terms.
Given an expression
e_{1}
of type
\tau_{1}
,
a pattern
T
that also has type
\tau_{1}
,
and two branches
e_{2}
and
e_{3}
,
the expression
\mathbf{case}\;e_{1}\;\mathbf{of}\;T\to e_{2}\;\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to e_{3}
is
given
type
\tau_{2}
.

The type system extended with linear implication,
as defined in
Section

3
, does not
yet
guarantee the preservation property,
and consequently, soundness.
In this section,
we first illustrate a case where soundness is violated
in
Section

4.1.1

Subsequently, we discuss
how
to prevent such unsoundness and
to establish type soundness
in
Section

4.2
.
and
in
Section

4.3
.

Consider the following expression, which ideally should not be typable as it leads to type inconsistency.

e_{\mathsf{DLfail}}

leads to an inconsistency
when applied to doubly-linked lists of length two and zero.

(90)

This discrepancy in return types demonstrates a lack of type consistency.
Since the type system should reject programs exhibiting such inconsistencies,
this expression should not be typable.

However, contrary to this expectation,
the program is
typable under the production rules
P_{\textsf{DL-LLT}}

(
2.2.1
) (
Section

2.2.1
)
within the type system introduced in
Section

3
.

To analyse the reason behind this,
we first present the
text version
of the program
e_{\mathsf{DLfail}}
(previously introduced
visually) as follows:

\displaystyle e_{\mathsf{DLfail}}\triangleq\begin{array}[]{l}(\lambda\,x[X,Y,Z]:\mathit{dbllist}(X,Y,Z).\\
\quad\mathbf{case}\;x[X,Y,Z]\;\mathbf{of}\\
\qquad\nu W_{1}W_{2}W_{3}W_{4}.(\\
\qquad\quad\mathrm{Cons}(W_{1},X,W_{2},Z),\\
\qquad\quad w[W_{1}]:\mathit{nat}(W_{1}),\\
\qquad\quad y[Z,W_{3},W_{4},W_{2}]:\\
\qquad\qquad(\mathit{lltree}(Y,W_{4},W_{3})\multimap\\
\qquad\qquad\quad\mathit{dbllist}(Z,Y,W_{2})\\
\qquad\qquad){\{Z,W_{3},W_{4},W_{2}\}},\\
\qquad\quad z[W_{4},Y,W_{3}]:\mathit{lltree}(Y,W_{4},W_{3})\\
\qquad)\to z[X,Y,Z]\\
\quad\>\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to\mathrm{Leaf}(0,Y,Z),X\bowtie Z\\
)(W).\end{array}

We demonstrate that the following type judgement
is successfully derived in the type derivation
presented in
\figref

\displaystyle\emptyset\vdash_{P_{\textsf{DL-LLT}}}e_{\mathsf{DLfail}}:(\mathit{dbllist}(X,Y,Z)\to\mathit{lltree}(X,Y,Z))(W).

(104)

In the type derivation in
\figref

the derivation of
\varphi(2)
,
corresponding to the right-hand side of the first
\to
in the case expression,
leads to a type inconsistency in the return values.
While this step results in the type inconsistency,
it is not the fundamental source of the problem.

The primary issue arises in the type derivation of the pattern in the case expression,
as captured by
\varphi(1)
.
Here, the type checking mechanism fails to
sufficiently enforce the expected types of subgraphs
that will be bound to
the graph variables
y[Z,W_{3},W_{2},W_{4}]
and
z[W_{4},Y,W_{3}]
.
In particular, the types of the subgraphs bound to these
graph variables will differ from
their expected annotated types,
leading to an unsound type derivation.

Typing Derivation of Unsound Typing Judgement (

)

This issue stems from a fundamental limitation in the type system,
which lacks a mechanism to ensure that a subgraph matched by a graph variable
is
always
of the expected annotated type.
Previous approaches relied on dynamic type checking
to enforce the correctness of subgraph bindings,
ensuring that the subgraph bound to
z[W_{4},Y,W_{3}]

conformed to the expected annotation
\mathit{lltree}(W_{4},Y,W_{3})
.
However, the objective of this study is to establish a statically verifiable guarantee
without resorting to runtime type enforcement.

To resolve this issue,
we introduce additional constraints to ensure
that any subgraph matched by a graph variable conforms to the expected type.

In the following section,
we discuss the constraints
on
the pattern of case expressions
and constraints on the type system
that prevent this form of unsoundness.

4.1.2
Introduction of Restrictions

The key to ensuring the soundness of the type system
is the introduction of structural constraints
that enforce the types
of subgraphs matched in a case expression to be
uniquely determined.

The first essential constraint is to ensure that type production rules are disjoint:
each right-hand side of a production rule must contain exactly one constructor atom,
a node with a constructor name,
whose name is unique within the set of rules.
By enforcing disjointness,
every subgraph connected to a terminal atom is guaranteed
to have a uniquely determined type.

Furthermore,
in pattern matching,
we impose an additional constraint
that graph variables must not be directly connected to one another.
Instead, they must be connected via terminal atoms.
This constraint ensures that any subgraph matched by a graph variable
must necessarily pass through a terminal atom,
thereby guaranteeing the unique determination
of the type of the subgraph matching the graph variable.

We believe that the constraint on production rules
implies that the graphs must have bounded treewidth
and excludes certain classes of graphs.
However, we have found that even with this constraint,
useful types can still be expressed;
for example,
the production rules

P_{\textsf{DL-LLT}}
(
2.2.1
)
all satisfy these constraints.
Thus, we consider this as a reasonable and practical design choice.
Examining the relationship between this constraint and treewidth,
as well as exploring the possibility of relaxing it,
remains an open challenge for future research.

We also believe that
the constraints on patterns in case expressions
do not substantially limit
the expressiveness of the language.
All examples presented in

Section

2

and

Section

3

adhere to these constraints.
The program
e_{\mathsf{DLfail}}
shown in
(
4.1.1
)
intentionally violates these constraints;
however, it can be easily rewritten to comply with them
while preserving its semantics,
as demonstrated by
e_{\mathsf{DLfail}}^{\prime}

(
4.1.2
).
