In the expression
e_{\mathsf{DLfail}}^{\prime}
, since the tail of a
\mathrm{Cons}
atom,
a subgraph connected through its second argument,
is always of type
\mathit{dbllist}
,
any subgraph that matches the graph variable
z
must necessarily have the type

\mathit{dbllist}
.
Consequently, in the corrected example,
type derivation fails because the types of the graph variable
z
and
the
\mathrm{Leaf}
atom
both appearing on the right-hand sides of
\to
s in the case expression
do not align.

4.2
Formalisation of Static Constraints

In this section, we formalise the constraints on the structure of production rules
and on the patterns occurring in
case
expressions.

We impose restrictions on graphs to enable unique traversal through specific links.
We introduce the notion of
primary roots
for types, atoms, and graph variables.
We then impose additional restrictions so that, by traversing
these primary roots,
we obtain a unique spanning tree.
The introduction of primary roots effectively restricts the class of graphs
handled by
\lambda_{GT}
to connected graphs.

We refer to the last arguments of types, atoms, and graph variables as their

primary roots
, and we use
pr
to denote the function that extracts them.

Definition 4.2

(Primary Root)
.

\displaystyle\textit{pr}(\alpha(\dots,X))

\displaystyle\triangleq X

\displaystyle\textit{pr}((\tau\to\tau)(\dots,X))

\displaystyle\triangleq X

\displaystyle\textit{pr}((\dots\multimap\tau){\{\dots\}})

\displaystyle\triangleq\textit{pr}(\tau)

\displaystyle\textit{pr}(p(\dots,X))

\displaystyle\triangleq X

\displaystyle\textit{pr}(x[\dots,X]:\tau)

\displaystyle\triangleq X\text{ where }X=\textit{pr}(\tau)

∎

The primary root of a linear implication type is
the primary root of the type on the right-hand side of
\multimap
.
For a graph variable of the form
x[\dots,X]:\tau
,
if the link
X

is not the primary root of the annotated type
\tau
,
its primary root is undefined.

In what follows,
we require that the primary root always exists
for every type and variable.

We define a notation for expressing whether two links are
fused with given link fusions.

Definition 4.3

(Fusibility Relation)
.

Let
F=(W_{1}\bowtie U_{1},\dots,W_{n}\bowtie U_{n})
.

X\bowtie_{F}Y

denotes that

\langle X,Y\rangle\in R
,
where
R
is the smallest equivalence relation
that contains

\{\langle W_{1},U_{1}\rangle,\dots,\langle W_{n},U_{n}\rangle\}
.
∎

Note that identical links are always considered fused.

In order to distinguish primary roots from other links,
we must ensure that certain links are not fused with primary roots.
To this end, we define the set of links of type atoms
that may potentially be fused with primary roots
by applying production rules as follows:

Definition 4.4

(Links Fusible with Primary Roots)
.

\begin{array}[]{llll}\textit{fused2PR}((\tau\to\tau)(\overrightarrow{Y},X),P)\triangleq\{X\}\\
\textit{fused2PR}(\alpha(X_{1},\dots,X_{n}),P)\triangleq\\
\quad\{X_{i}\mid\\
\qquad\bigl(\alpha(Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n})\longrightarrow\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{V}),\overrightarrow{W\bowtie U},\overrightarrow{\tau})\bigr)\in P\\
\qquad\land\,Y_{i}\bowtie_{\overrightarrow{W\bowtie U}}Y_{n}\\
\quad\}\\
\end{array}

∎

In the case of an arrow type
(\tau\to\tau)(\overrightarrow{Y},X)
,
no further production rules are applied,
and thus the primary root will not be fused with any other links.
Therefore, the resulting set simply consists of the primary root
X
.

For type variables, the situation is more complex.
The resulting set consists of a subset
containing the
i
-th link
X_{i}
of the type variable.
Here, the index
i
corresponds to the position of the link
for which there exists a production rule

\alpha(Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n})\longrightarrow\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{V}),\overrightarrow{W\bowtie U},\overrightarrow{\tau})

such that the
i
-th link
Y_{i}
and the primary root
Y_{n}

of the type atom
\alpha(Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n})
on the left-hand side
LHS of the rule
are fused together on the right-hand side RHS of the rule
by
\overrightarrow{W\bowtie U}
.

Note that the sets of link names obtained by
\textit{fused2PR}(\tau,P)

naturally include the primary roots of
\tau
.

Using the notations defined above,

Definition

4.5
states the constraints imposed on production rules.

Definition 4.5

(Restriction on Production Rules)
.

Each production rule in
P

must take the following form:

\alpha(\overrightarrow{W},X)\longrightarrow\nu\overrightarrow{Y}.(C(\overrightarrow{Z},X),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V},\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{n})

and must satisfy the following conditions
as well as the conditions given in
Definition

2.7
:

1.

X\notin\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}
;

2.

\textit{pr}(\tau_{i})\in\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}
for all
i
;

3.

for all
i\neq j
,

if

X_{i}\in\textit{fused2PR}(\tau_{i},P)\land X_{j}\in\textit{fused2PR}(\tau_{j},P)

then

\neg X_{i}\bowtie_{\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}}X_{j}\land\neg X_{i}\bowtie_{\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}}X
;

4.

the constructor name
C
must be unique within the set
P

of production rules.

∎

Condition (1) ensures that
X
is a free link
so that the primary root
X
can be reached from outside.

Condition (2) ensures that the subsequent types
\overrightarrow{\tau}

(i.e., the types of subcomponents reachable from a constructor)
are connected to the constructor atom
C(\overrightarrow{Z},X)
.

Condition (3) ensures that each of its subcomponents
can be traversed uniquely once the constructor atom
C
is reached.
One might think that, with respect to Condition (3), the simple requirement

\textit{pr}(\tau_{i})\neq\textit{pr}(\tau_{j})
for all
i\neq j
would suffice.
However, this condition is insufficient
because it still allows the possibility
that the primary roots
\textit{pr}(\tau_{i})
and
\textit{pr}(\tau_{j})

could be fused at a later stage by the application of production rules.
Condition (3) is therefore defined using
fused2PR
.

We show that the production rules
P_{\textsf{DL-LLT}}
(
2.2.1
)
satisfy Condition (3) in
Example

4.6
and
Example

4.7
below.

Example 4.6

(Doubly-Linked Lists)
.

The production rules of
\mathit{dbllist}
in
P_{\textsf{DL-LLT}}

(
2.2.1
)
are as follows:

\displaystyle\mathit{dbllist}(X,Y,Z)\longrightarrow{}

\displaystyle\quad\;\;\mathrm{Nil}(X,Z),Y\bowtie Z

(110)

\displaystyle\quad\mid\nu W_{1}W_{2}.(\mathrm{Cons}(W_{1},X,W_{2},Z),{}

\displaystyle\qquad\mathit{nat}(W_{1}),\mathit{dbllist}(Z,Y,W_{2})).

(111)

For the first production rule (
110
),
since no type atom occurs on the right-hand side,
Condition (3) is trivially satisfied.
For the second production rule (
111
), we have

\begin{array}[]{llll}\textit{fused2PR}(\mathit{nat}(W_{1}),P)=\{W_{1}\},\\
\textit{fused2PR}(\mathit{dbllist}(Z,Y,W_{2}),P)=\{Y,W_{2}\}.\end{array}

This production rule has no fusion,
and the sets
\{W_{1}\}
,
\{Y,W_{2}\}
, and
\{X\}
are pairwise disjoint.
Therefore, this production rule satisfies Condition (3).

Example 4.7

(Leaf-Linked Trees)
.

The production rules of
\mathit{lltree}
in
P_{\textsf{DL-LLT}}

(
2.2.1
)
are as follows:

\displaystyle\mathit{lltree}(L,R,X)\longrightarrow{}

\displaystyle\quad\;\;\nu W_{1}.(\mathrm{Leaf}(W_{1},R,X),L\bowtie X,\mathit{nat}(W_{1}))

(112)

\displaystyle\quad\mid\nu W_{1}.(\mathrm{LeafM}(W_{1},R,X),L\bowtie X,\mathit{nat}(W_{1}))

(113)

\displaystyle\quad\mid\nu YW_{1}W_{2}.(\mathrm{Node}(W_{1},W_{2},X),{}

\displaystyle\qquad\mathit{lltree}(L,Y,W_{1}),\mathit{lltree}(Y,R,W_{1})).

(114)

For the first and second production rules
(
112
)(
113
),
we have

\textit{fused2PR}(\mathit{nat}(W_{1}),P)=\{W_{1}\},

where
W_{1}\in\{W_{1}\}
and
X
do
not satisfy
W_{1}\bowtie_{L\bowtie X}X
.
Therefore, these production rules satisfy Condition (3).
For the third production rule (
114
), we have

\begin{array}[]{llll}\textit{fused2PR}(\mathit{lltree}(L,Y,W_{1}),P)=\{L,W_{1}\},\\
\textit{fused2PR}(\mathit{lltree}(Y,R,W_{2}),P)=\{Y,W_{2}\}.\\
\end{array}

This production rule has no fusion,
and the sets
\{L,W_{1}\}
,
\{Y,W_{2}\}
, and
\{X\}
are pairwise disjoint.
Therefore, this production rule satisfies Condition (3).

Condition (4) is intended to uniquely determine both
the type of a graph whose root is a constructor atom
and the types of the subgraphs connected to that constructor atom.

We also impose a constraint on patterns in
case
expressions.
We first define the syntax of
restricted templates
,
which will be used to describe the patterns.

Definition 4.8

(Case Pattern Syntax)
.

The syntax of restricted templates
\mathcal{T}
is
defined recursively as follows:

\begin{array}[]{lcll}\mathcal{T}&::=&\nu\overrightarrow{Y}.(x[\overrightarrow{Z},X]:\tau,\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{1},\dots,\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{n})\mid\widehat{\mathcal{T}}&\quad(n\geq 0),\\
\widehat{\mathcal{T}}&::=&\nu\overrightarrow{Y}.(C(\overrightarrow{Z},X),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V},\mathcal{T}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{T}_{n})&\quad(n\geq 0).\\
\end{array}

∎

The template
\widehat{\mathcal{T}}
denotes a template whose root contains a
constructor atom,
whereas the template
\mathcal{T}
allows a graph variable at the root.
When the root of a template is a graph variable,
its subtemplates must have constructor atoms at their root.
Note that the above definition allows two or more
constructor atoms to occur
consecutively.

To obtain the primary root of the leftmost graph variable or constructor atom
in restricted templates
\mathcal{T}
,
we extend
pr
as follows:

\displaystyle\textit{pr}(\nu\overrightarrow{Y}.(x[\overrightarrow{Z},X]:\tau,\dots))

\displaystyle\triangleq X,

\displaystyle\textit{pr}(\nu\overrightarrow{Y}.(C(\overrightarrow{Z},X),\dots))

\displaystyle\triangleq X.

The constraint on links for case
patterns is formally defined as follows.

Definition 4.9

(Case Pattern Link Constraints)
.

The pattern
\mathcal{T}
is required to satisfy
\mathit{patCond}(\mathcal{T})

defined recursively as follows:

\displaystyle\mathit{patCond}(\nu\overrightarrow{Y}.(x[\overrightarrow{Z},X]:\tau,\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{1},\dots,\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{n}))\triangleq{}

\displaystyle\quad X\notin\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}

(115)

\displaystyle\quad\land\;\bigl(\forall i,j\in\{1,\dots,n\}.\;i\neq j\implies{}

\displaystyle\quad\qquad\textit{pr}(\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{i})\in\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}

(116)

\displaystyle\quad\qquad\land\;\mathit{varLinks}(\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{i})\cap\mathit{varLinks}(\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{j})=\emptyset

(117)

\displaystyle\quad\qquad\land\;\mathit{patCond}(\widehat{\mathcal{T}}_{i})\bigr),

(118)

\displaystyle\mathit{patCond}(\nu\overrightarrow{Y}.(C(\overrightarrow{Z},X),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V},\mathcal{T}_{1},\dots,\mathcal{T}_{n}))\triangleq{}

\displaystyle\quad X\notin\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}

(119)

\displaystyle\quad\land\;\bigl(\forall i,j\in\{1,\dots,n\}.\;i\neq j\implies{}

\displaystyle\quad\qquad\textit{pr}(\mathcal{T}_{i})\in\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}

(120)

\displaystyle\quad\qquad\land\;\mathit{varLinks}(\mathcal{T}_{i})\cap\mathit{varLinks}(\mathcal{T}_{j})=\emptyset

(121)

\displaystyle\quad\qquad\land\;\mathit{patCond}(\mathcal{T}_{i})\bigr),

(122)

where
\mathit{varLinks}
is defined recursively as follows:

\displaystyle\mathit{varLinks}(\nu\overrightarrow{Y}.(x[\overrightarrow{Z}]:\tau,\overrightarrow{\widehat{\mathcal{T}}}))\triangleq{}

\displaystyle\quad\bigl(\bigcup_{\widehat{\mathcal{T}}\in\overrightarrow{\widehat{\mathcal{T}}}}\textit{pr}(\widehat{\mathcal{T}})\cup\mathit{varLinks}(\widehat{\mathcal{T}})\bigr)\setminus\{\overrightarrow{Y}\},

(123)

\displaystyle\mathit{varLinks}(\nu\overrightarrow{Y}.(C(\overrightarrow{Z}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V},\overrightarrow{\mathcal{T}}))\triangleq{}

\displaystyle\quad\left\{X\,\middle|\,X\bowtie_{\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}}W\land W\in\bigcup_{\mathcal{T}\in\overrightarrow{\mathcal{T}}}\mathit{varLinks}(\mathcal{T})\right\}\setminus\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}.

(124)

∎

\mathit{varLinks}

(
123
)(
124
)
collects the set of graph-variable links
that occur free and are either
the primary links of constructor atoms in their subtemplates
or links fused with such links.
The definition proceeds as follows:

1.

for a template whose root is a graph variable,
it collects the primary roots of its subtemplates
and recurses (
123
),
while eliminating hidden links;

2.

for a template whose root is a constructor atom,
it recursively collects the links therein
and collects the links that can be fused with them
(
124
),
while eliminating hidden links.

Using
\mathit{varLinks}
,
\mathit{patCond}
of
Definition

4.9

checks that a template satisfies the following properties:

1.

the primary root of the leftmost graph variable
or constructor atom is a free link (
115
)(
119
);

2.

each subtemplate is connected to the
leftmost graph variable or constructor atom
through its primary root (
116
)(
120
);

3.

separation condition:

the links in subtemplates
that occur free in the arguments of graph variables
and are connected to the primary roots of subtemplates
of the graph variables
are pairwise disjoint
(
117
)(
121
); and

4.

this property is checked recursively
(
118
)(
122
).

The purpose of the case pattern syntax
(
Definition

4.8
)
and its link conditions
(
Definition

4.9
)
is to guarantee the type safety of pattern matching in case expressions;
that is, whenever pattern matching succeeds,
the type assigned to each graph variable
is identical to the type of the subgraph that matches it.
To achieve this,
the constraints guarantee that,
for both the type of a graph variable and that of the corresponding matching subgraph,
the types occurring on
the LHS and the RHS
of the linear implication (
\multimap
) are identical.
Here, the
LHS
only needs to coincide up to multiset equivalence.
When the type is not a linear implication,
only the argument for
the RHS is relevant.

The case pattern syntax
(
Definition

4.8
)
and its link conditions
(
Definition

4.9
)
ensure these properties as follows:

LHS of
\multimap
:

According to the syntactic conditions
of

Definition

4.8

and the link condition
(
115
),
every subtemplate connected to a graph variable via its primary root
has a constructor atom at its root.
Thus, by the constraints on production rules
(
Definition

4.5
),
the types of these subtemplates
and those of their corresponding matching subgraphs
are uniquely determined.

However, even if the types of these subtemplates
and their matching subgraphs are uniquely determined,
ambiguity may still arise when a subtemplate
connected to the primary root of a graph variable
is shared among other graph variables.
To prevent this,
the separation condition enforced by
\mathit{varLinks}

(
117
)(
121
)
requires that
the subtemplates of graph variables
must not shared with other graph variables
through their primary roots.

RHS of
\multimap
:

The syntactic conditions in

Definition

4.8
,
together with the link conditions other than
\mathit{varLinks}

in
Definition

4.9

(
115
)(
119
)(
116
)(
120
)
require that
the primary root of each graph variable
either (i) be connected to a constructor atom
or (ii) serve as the primary root of the entire case pattern.
For Case (i),
by the constraints on production rules
(
Definition

4.5
),
the type of the subtemplate and its matching subgraph
are uniquely determined.
For Case (ii),

Ty-Case
in
Definition

4.1
(and

Definition

4.11
coming later) ensures that
the type of the case pattern coincides with
the type of the scrutinee
to be evaluated and
its evaluation result, i.e.,
the graph being matched.

We allow only patterns in
case
expressions
that are structurally congruent to a template that follows
Definition

4.8

and satisfy Case Pattern Link Conditions given in
Definition

4.9
.

For example,

e_{\mathsf{DLfail}}^{\prime}
(
4.1.2
)
(
Section

4.1.2
)
satisfies the constraints of

Definition

4.8
and
Definition

4.9
.
The case pattern of
e_{\mathsf{DLfail}}^{\prime}

is congruent to

\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{DLfail}}^{\prime}\triangleq\begin{array}[]{lll}\nu W_{2}W_{3}.(y[X,W_{3},W_{2},Z]:\\
\qquad(\mathit{lltree}(W_{3},Y,W_{4})\multimap\\
\qquad\quad\mathit{dbllist}(X,Y,Z)\\
\qquad){\{X,W_{3},W_{2},Z\}},\\
\quad\nu W_{1}W_{4}.(\mathrm{Cons}(W_{1},W_{2},W_{4},W_{3}),\\
\qquad w[W_{1}]:\mathit{nat}(W_{1}),\\
\qquad z[W_{3},Y,W_{4}]:\mathit{lltree}(W_{3},Y,W_{4})\\
\quad)\\
).\end{array}

Here, the graph variables
y[X,W_{3},W_{2},Z]
and
z[W_{3},Y,W_{4}]
do not
occur consecutively,
and the pattern
\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{DLfail}}^{\prime}
satisfies the syntactic conditions
specified in
Definition

4.8
.
It also satisfies the link conditions defined in
Definition

4.9
.
In particular,
the primary root
W_{4}
of the graph variable
z[W_{3},Y,W_{4}]

is connected to the constructor atom
\mathrm{Cons}(W_{1},W_{2},W_{4},W_{3})

as required by (
120
),
and it trivially satisfies the separation condition
since
\mathit{varLinks}
always returns an empty set.

On the other hand,

e_{\mathsf{DLfail}}
(defined in (
4.1.1
))
does not satisfy the constraints of
Definition

4.8
and
Definition

4.9
.
The case pattern of
e_{\mathsf{DLfail}}
is congruent to

\displaystyle\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{DLfail}}\triangleq\begin{array}[]{lll}\nu W_{1}W_{2}.(\mathrm{Cons}(W_{1},X,W_{2},Z),\\
\quad w[W_{1}]:\mathit{nat}(W_{1}),\\
\quad\nu W_{3}W_{4}.(y[Z,W_{3},W_{4},W_{2}]:\\
\quad\qquad(\mathit{lltree}(Y,W_{4},W_{3})\multimap\\
\quad\qquad\quad\mathit{dbllist}(Z,Y,W_{2})\\
\quad\qquad){\{Z,W_{3},W_{4},W_{2}\}},\\
\qquad z[W_{4},Y,W_{3}]:\mathit{lltree}(Y,W_{4},W_{3})\\
\quad)\\
).\end{array}

However,
\mathcal{T}_{\mathsf{DLfail}}
does not satisfy the syntactic condition
in
Definition

4.8
,
because the graph variables
y[Z,W_{3},W_{4},W_{2}]
and
z[W_{4},Y,W_{3}]

occur consecutively.
Since the graph variable
z[W_{4},Y,W_{3}]
has its primary root
W_{3}

connected only to
y[Z,W_{3},W_{4},W_{2}]
and not to any constructor atom,
even if we rearrange the order of the constructor atom
\mathrm{Cons}(W_{1},X,W_{2},Z)

and the graph variables
y[Z,W_{3},W_{4},W_{2}]
and
z[W_{4},Y,W_{3}]
,
the pattern still fails to satisfy the link conditions
(
120
) of

Definition

4.9
.

To represent typing derivations that involve only certain typing rules,
we define the following typing relation.

Definition 4.10

(Subset Type System)
.

Let
S
be
a subset of the set of the typing rules.

\Gamma\vdash_{P}^{S}e:\tau

denotes that

\Gamma\vdash_{P}e:\tau

can be derived only using typing rules in
S
.
∎

The revised typing rule for
case
expressions is given as follows:

Definition 4.11

(Revised
Ty-Case
with Pattern Constraints)
.

\begin{array}[]{c}\Gamma\vdash_{P}e_{1}:\tau_{1}\\
\Gamma,\mathit{vt}(T)\vdash_{P}e_{2}:\tau_{2}\end{array}

\begin{array}[]{c}\mathit{vt}(T)\vdash_{P}^{S}\mathcal{T}:\tau_{1}\\
\Gamma\vdash_{P}e_{3}:\tau_{2}\end{array}

Ty-Case

\Gamma\vdash_{P}(\mathbf{case}\;e_{1}\;\mathbf{of}\;T\to e_{2}\;\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to e_{3}):\tau_{2}

where
\mathcal{T}\equiv T
,

\mathit{patCond}(\mathcal{T})
, and

S=\{\textsf{Ty-Prod}{},\textsf{Ty-Alpha}{},\textsf{Ty-Var}{},\textsf{Ty-LI-E}{}\}
.
∎

This revised
Ty-Case
allows only patterns in
case
expressions
that are structurally congruent to the template
\mathcal{T}
,
whose syntax is defined in
Definition

4.8

and which must satisfy the link constraints given in
Definition

4.9
.

Importantly,
these constraints
(
Definitions

4.5
,
4.8
and
4.9
)
do not significantly compromise the expressiveness of the language.
Most of the data types and operations illustrated in
\Cite
sano2023
remain expressible within this restricted framework.
Moreover,
the constrained language still supports algebraic data types,
as in conventional functional languages,
and additionally allows graph-shaped data structures with sharing and cycles.
Hence, it is more expressive than conventional functional languages with respect to data representation.

4.3
Proof Sketch of Soundness

We conjecture that the type system described in
Section

4.2
,
obtained by imposing the constraints of

Definition

4.5
and
Definition

4.11
, is sound.
Here, we only discuss a proof sketch.

This statement is formalised as follows.

Proposition 4.12

(Preservation)
.

If

\Gamma\vdash_{P}e:\tau

and

e\>\longrightarrow_{\mathit{val}}\>e^{\prime}
,
then

\Gamma\vdash_{P}e^{\prime}:\tau

In what follows, we outline a proof sketch of
4.12
.

In the system described in
Section

4.2
,
dynamic checks in
case
expressions are eliminated.
It is therefore necessary to argue that the properties previously guaranteed
by dynamic checks are instead ensured statically.

More concretely, we consider the following proposition.

Proposition 4.13

(Matching Type Consistency)
.

Let
e
be an expression
(\mathbf{case}\;G\;\mathbf{of}\;T\to e_{1}\;\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to e_{2})

and
\overrightarrow{\theta}
be graph substitutions.
If
e
is typable
and

G\equiv T\overrightarrow{\theta}
,
then

\emptyset\vdash_{P}x[\overrightarrow{X}]\overrightarrow{\theta}:\tau

for all
x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau\in\mathit{vt}(T)
.

Intuitively, this proposition expresses that
if a subgraph matches a graph variable in a
case
expression,
the type of that subgraph must coincide with the type assigned to the graph variable.

To argue for this property, we proceed in two main steps.
First, we observe that any graph (value) matched in a
case
expression
can be transformed into a congruent
Normal Form
,
and that this normal form is unique.
Then, we analyse the matching process between templates and
matching graphs in their Normal Forms,
divide it into two exhaustive cases,
and argue that the property holds in each case.

We begin by defining the notion of a
Normal Form
for graphs.

Definition 4.14

(Normal Form)
.

Let
G
be a typable graph whose type is not a linear implication type,
and whose typing derivation uses only
Ty-Prod

in derivations without premises of
Ty-Arrow
.
Then the graph
G
is said to be in
Normal Form
.
A graph is said to have a Normal Form
if it is congruent to a graph that is in Normal Form.
∎

Since the use of
Ty-Cong
is excluded from derivations,
the Normal Form of any set of congruent graphs is syntactically unique,
up to
\alpha
-renaming of local links.
This implies that the spanning tree of the graph whose
backbone is formed by primary roots
is uniquely determined.

We state that every typable graph (value) whose type is not a linear implication
has a unique Normal Form, up to
\alpha
-renaming of local link names.
We first state the existence of a Normal Form for such graphs.

Proposition 4.15

(Existence of a Normal Form)
.

Let
G
be a typable graph whose type is not a linear implication type.
Then, there exists a congruent graph
G^{\prime}

whose
typing derivation
uses only
Ty-Prod
in
the derivation
without premises of
Ty-Arrow
.

Next, we state the uniqueness of the Normal Form.

Proposition 4.16

(Uniqueness of a Normal Form)
.

Let
G
and
G^{\prime}
be graphs in Normal Form such that
G\equiv G^{\prime}
.
Then
G
and
G^{\prime}
share the same typing derivation
among those that contain no premises of
Ty-Arrow
.

The proofs of
4.15
and
4.16

are provided in Appendices
D
and
D.2
.

Using
4.15
and
4.16
,
we give a proof sketch of
4.13
below.

Proof sketch of
4.13
.

Consider the case expression

(\mathbf{case}\;G\;\mathbf{of}\;T\to e_{1}\;\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to e_{2})
.
Suppose that both
G
and
T
have the type
\tau
.
Since the matching target graph in a
case
expression
is typable,
and because in
Section

3.1
we imposed the restriction that
the type of the first argument of a
case
expression
must not be a linear implication type,
we can consider a Normal Form for the graph.

We now analyse template-graph matching in the following
two cases.

1.

A graph variable appears at the root of a graph,
that is,
the graph variable has a root link which is the root link of the type of a graph.

By the typing rule Ty-Case,
the types of the expression
e_{1}
and the template
T
must be identical.
Therefore, by the induction hypothesis,
the graph reduced from
e_{1}
has the same type as
T
.

At this point, we consider two cases.

(a)

If
T
consists of only a graph variable,
then the type of the graph variable corresponds directly to the type of
T
,
which is also the type of the pattern being matched.

(b)

On the other hand, if
T
is not solely a graph variable,
the typing must be derived using the rule Ty-LI-E.
According to
Definition

4.11
and
Definition

4.5
,
the root of each sub-spanning tree connected to the graph variable in
T

and those matches in
G

contains exactly the same constructor atom.

As a result, the type of these sub-spanning trees remains consistent.
Therefore,
the type of the graph variable obtained by subtracting
the types of sub-spanning tree from the overall types
in both
T
and the reduced graph
G

must be the same type.

2.

The graph variable does not appear at the root of the graph.

We consider a sub-template containing a graph variable:

T\triangleq\nu\overrightarrow{Y}.(x[\overrightarrow{Z},X],\overrightarrow{\widehat{\mathcal{T}}}).

According to
Definition

4.11
,
the graph variable must be located immediately under a constructor atom of the form

C(\dots,X,\dots)
, where
X
is the root link of the graph variable.

During matching, this constructor atom is expected to correspond to
an identical constructor atom
C(\dots,X,\dots)
in the target graph
G
.
Since
G
is assumed to admit a unique spanning tree,
the sub-spanning tree of
G
that matches the sub-template must be
the one connected to
X
via this constructor atom.

At this point, we analyse the type consistency.
Because of the disjointness constraint on the production rules,
there exists a unique production rule that can be applied to any given constructor atom
via the typing rule
Ty-Prod
.
Therefore, the type of the sub-template
T
and that of the corresponding subgraph in
G

must be identical.

Finally
we consider the cases whether the sub-template consists solely
of a graph variable or not.
In either case, the conclusion remains the same as in Case (1).

∎

Proof sketch of
4.12
.

The preservation property stated in
4.12

can be established straightforwardly
using the proof of
Section

3.5
,
with
4.13
.
∎

The soundness of the type system is established by
4.12
,
in combination with the progress lemma which
can be established straightforwardly from

Section

3.5
.

5
Related Work

In this section, we discuss related work and highlight key differences.

5.1
Advancements Over Prior Work on
\lambda_{GT}

Earlier work on
\lambda_{GT}

[
28
]
[
27
]
required
runtime type checking in
case
expressions.
In this study, we seek
static
type checking,
eliminating the need for dynamic checks and ensuring a statically sound language design.

A key contribution in this work is the introduction of

linear implication types
(
\multimap
)
to the prior type system of
\lambda_{GT}
.
This mechanism enables the typing of incomplete data structures,
which is inspired by the
Magic Wand
operator in Separation Logic
[
18
]

and the
Difference Type
in LMNtalGG
[
33
]
.

The difference between the
proposed linear implication types
and the Magic Wand and the Difference Types is an explicit representation of free links.
Unlike in Separation Logic, where free links are not explicitly tracked,
our framework, which relies on hyperlinks, requires explicit
handling of free links.
Similarly, while LMNtalGG
does not require the explicit handling of free links due to its non-hypergraph setting,
our approach mandates their explicit declaration
to accommodate hypergraph-based data structures.

Another major refinement in our work is the introduction of
language-level constraints
alongside type system restrictions to ensure soundness.
The mere addition of an operator analogous to the Magic Wand does not guarantee soundness.
Thus, constraints are imposed not only on the type system but also on the language syntax,
particularly in
case
patterns, to maintain correctness.
This approach contrasts with Disjoint LMNtalGG
[
33
]
,
which relies on dynamic type checks, whereas our approach ensures static type checking.

5.2
Comparison with Other Existing Research

Ownership type systems
[
4
]
and affine/linear type systems
help manage destructive memory operations preventing common pitfalls
such as memory leaks and dangling pointers.
However, these approaches alone
cannot handle data structures
involving shared or cyclic references.

Separation Logic
[
22
]
[
21
]
and shape
analysis
[
32
]
have been extensively studied for verifying
pointer-manipulating programs.
While powerful in principle, they often require
specialised knowledge of specification formalisms (e.g., symbolic heaps and
inductive predicates
[
19
]
[
20
]
[
6
]
[
12
]
),
making them difficult for general programmers to adopt.

Graph Types
[
14
]
provide a means of defining canonical spanning trees
with
auxiliary edges
described by routing expressions (regular path
specifications).
In contrast,

\lambda_{GT}
directly manipulates graphs
using powerful pattern matching inspired by graph transformation,
rather than accessing nodes via routing expressions.

Numerous graph transformation languages and frameworks
(e.g.,
[
10
]
[
24
]
[
15
]
[
1
]
[
11
]
[
13
]
[
30
]
[
31
]
[
8
]
[
29
]
)
have been developed, yet their integration into a functional paradigm remains a challenge.
In particular,
verifying the correctness of pattern matching statically
is difficult due to the complexity of graphs.
We address this issue by
incorporating linear implication types into the type system of
\lambda_{GT}
.

Conventional functional languages (e.g., Haskell, OCaml) typically process
tree-shaped data with potential sharing using
let rec
definitions
or built-in reference types.
However, these mechanisms do not inherently
enforce structural shape constraints.
Several approaches (e.g., Clean
[
2
]
, Inductive Graphs
[
7
]
)
employ graph-based representations internally,
but they still primarily treat data as trees within the type system.
UnCAL
[
3
]
and FUnCAL
[
16
]

supports functional queries on graph databases based on bisimulation;
however this differs significantly from the pattern matching mechanism in
\lambda_{GT}
.

Context patterns in Haskell
[
17
]
extend conventional pattern matching
by enabling not only the matching of subtrees
but also the matching of the surrounding context from which the subtrees are removed.
This context is represented as a function,
allowing for its reuse in subsequent computation.
This capability closely resembles the kind of structural decomposition targeted in
\lambda_{GT}
.
However, a key difference lies in the underlying data structures:
while
\lambda_{GT}
supports graphs including doubly-linked lists and leaf-linked trees,
contextual patterns are strictly limited to trees and their corresponding contexts.

6
Conclusion and Future Work

Enabling intuitive and safe manipulation of complex data structures
is a fundamental challenge in designing a programming language.
The
\lambda_{GT}
language, a purely functional programming language
that treats graphs as primary data structure,
addresses some of these challenges.
By abstracting data with shared references and cycles as graphs,
it enables intuitive operations through pattern matching.
The language also comes with its type system to guarantee the safety
of these operations.

However, some open challenges for the type system were identified in
previous work.
This study addresses these challenges by incorporating linear implication
into the
\lambda_{GT}
type system
and introducing new constraints to maintain soundness.

The extended type system allows typing of
incomplete graphs
,
that is, graphs in which some elements are missing from the graphs of user-defined types.
This type system
can handle structures such as a doubly-linked list missing one or more tail nodes,
or a leaf-linked tree with one or more absent leaves,
without requiring separate type definitions for such partial structures.
With this type system,
programs that perform operations involving these structures as intermediate values
can now be fully statically typed without additional effort from the user.

Future work on the technical side includes the handling of graphs with
free links and fusions only (i.e., graphs with no atoms) such as empty
difference lists (a.k.a. graph segments). Although they are quite
important in practice, subtlety of their
handling is somewhat similar to the handling of empty strings in
formal grammar and would require special care. Also,
graph structures with linear implication types are not yet allowed to
occur everywhere, and identifying and allowing more use cases of
linear implication types is our challenging future work.

Future work on a broader perspective
includes implementing a type checker and extending the type system,
such as incorporating polymorphic types and type inference.
Such enhancements would further improve the expressiveness and
usability of
\lambda_{GT}
,
paving the way for broader adoption of declarative operations
over complex data structures in purely functional programming paradigms.

Appendix A
Formal Definitions of Substitutions

We define two forms of capture-avoiding substitution: link
substitution and graph substitution.

Definition A.1

(Link Substitution)
.

A
link substitution
,

T\langle Z_{1},\dots,Z_{n}/Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n}\rangle
,
that replaces all free occurrences of

Y_{i}
with
Z_{i}

is defined as
in
\figref
table:hyperlink-substitution.
Here, the
Y_{1},\dots,Y_{n}
should be pairwise distinct.
Note that, if a free occurrence of
Y_{i}
occurs at a
location where
Z_{i}
would not be free,

\alpha
-conversion may be required.

\textbf{0}\langle\overrightarrow{Z}/\overrightarrow{Y}\rangle

\triangleq

0

p(\overrightarrow{X})\langle\overrightarrow{Z}/\overrightarrow{Y}\rangle

\triangleq

p(X_{1}\langle\overrightarrow{Z}/\overrightarrow{Y}\rangle,\ldots,X_{n}\langle\overrightarrow{Z}/\overrightarrow{Y}\rangle)

where
X\langle\overrightarrow{Z}/\overrightarrow{Y}\rangle=\left\{\begin{array}[]{@{}ll}Z_{i}&\mbox{if }X=Y_{i}\\
X&\mbox{if }X\notin\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\end{array}\right.

x[\overrightarrow{X}]\langle\overrightarrow{Z}/\overrightarrow{Y}\rangle

\triangleq

x[X_{1}\langle\overrightarrow{Z}/\overrightarrow{Y}\rangle,\ldots,X_{n}\langle\overrightarrow{Z}/\overrightarrow{Y}\rangle]

where
X\langle\overrightarrow{Z}/\overrightarrow{Y}\rangle=\left\{\begin{array}[]{@{}ll}Z_{i}&\mbox{if }X=Y_{i}\\
X&\mbox{if }X\notin\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\end{array}\right.

(T_{1},T_{2})\langle\overrightarrow{Z}/\overrightarrow{Y}\rangle

\triangleq

(T_{1}\langle\overrightarrow{Z}/\overrightarrow{Y}\rangle,T_{2}\langle\overrightarrow{Z}/\overrightarrow{Y}\rangle)

(\nu X.T)\langle\overrightarrow{Z}/\overrightarrow{Y}\rangle

\triangleq

\left\{\begin{array}[]{@{}ll}\nu X.T\langle\overrightarrow{Z^{\prime}}/\overrightarrow{Y^{\prime}}\rangle&\mbox{if }X=Y_{i}\ \land\\
&\overrightarrow{Z^{\prime}}=Z_{1},\dots,Z_{i-1},Z_{i+1},\dots,Z_{n}\\
&\overrightarrow{Y^{\prime}}=Y_{1},\dots,Y_{i-1},Y_{i+1},\dots,Y_{n}\\[1.0pt]
\nu X.T\langle\overrightarrow{Z}/\overrightarrow{Y}\rangle&\mbox{if }X\notin\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\land X\notin\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}\\[3.0pt]
\nu W.(T\langle W/X\rangle)\langle\overrightarrow{Z}/\overrightarrow{Y}\rangle&\mbox{if }X\notin\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\land X\in\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}\\
&\land W\notin\mathit{fn}(T)\land W\notin\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}\end{array}\right.

Figure 15:
(Hyper)link Substitution

∎

Before defining graph substitution, we define the notion of
free
functors
, where a functor, written
x/n
,
stands for the name
x
of a graph variable
x[\overrightarrow{X}]

with its arity
n
which is equal to
|\overrightarrow{X}|
.
We regard two graph variables with the same name and the
same arity and within the same scope as referring to the same variable
with possibly renamed free links.

Definition A.2

(Free functors of an expression)
.

We define free functors of an expression
e
,
\mathit{ff}(e)
,
in
\figref
table:free-functor.

\mathit{ff}(\mathbf{case}\;e_{1}\;\mathbf{of}\;T\to e_{2}\;\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to e_{3})\triangleq

\mathit{ff}(e_{1})\cup(\mathit{ff}(e_{2})\setminus\mathit{ff}(T))\cup\mathit{ff}(e_{3})

\mathit{ff}((e_{1}\;e_{2}))

\triangleq

\mathit{ff}(e_{1})\cup\mathit{ff}(e_{2})

\mathit{ff}(x[\overrightarrow{X}])

\triangleq

\{x/\lvert\overrightarrow{X}\rvert\}

\mathit{ff}(v\,(\overrightarrow{X}))

\triangleq

\emptyset

\mathit{ff}((\lambda\,x[\overrightarrow{X}].e)(\overrightarrow{Y}))

\triangleq

\mathit{ff}(e)\setminus\{x/\lvert\overrightarrow{X}\rvert\}

\mathit{ff}((T_{1},T_{2}))

\triangleq

\mathit{ff}(T_{1})\cup\mathit{ff}(T_{2})

\mathit{ff}(\nu X.T)

\triangleq

\mathit{ff}(T)

Figure 16:
Free functors of an expression

∎

Free functors are not to be confused with free link names.

Definition A.3

(Graph Substitution)
.

We define capture-avoiding substitution

\theta

of a graph variable

x[\overrightarrow{X}]

with a template
T

in
e
,
written
e[T/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]
,
as in
\figref
table:graph-substitution.
The definition is standard except that it handles the substitution of
the free links of graph variables in the third rule.
∎

(T_{1},T_{2})\theta

\triangleq

(T_{1}\theta,T_{2}\theta)

(\nu X.T)\theta

\triangleq

\nu X.T\theta

(x[\overrightarrow{X}])[T/y[\overrightarrow{Y}]]

\triangleq

if
x/\lvert\overrightarrow{X}\rvert=y/\lvert\overrightarrow{Y}\rvert
then
T{\langle\overrightarrow{X}/\overrightarrow{Y}\rangle}
else
x[\overrightarrow{X}]

(C(\overrightarrow{X}))\theta

\triangleq

C(\overrightarrow{X})

((\lambda\,x[\overrightarrow{X}].e)(\overrightarrow{Z}))[T/y[\overrightarrow{Y}]]~\triangleq

if

x/\lvert\overrightarrow{X}\rvert=y/\lvert\overrightarrow{Y}\rvert
then

(\lambda\,x[\overrightarrow{X}].e)(\overrightarrow{Z})

else if
x/\lvert\overrightarrow{X}\rvert\notin\mathit{ff}(T)
then

(\lambda\,x[\overrightarrow{X}].e[T/y[\overrightarrow{Y}]])(\overrightarrow{Z})

else

(\lambda\,z[\overrightarrow{X}].e[z[\overrightarrow{X}]/x[\overrightarrow{X}]][T/y[\overrightarrow{Y}]])(\overrightarrow{Z})

where

z/\lvert\overrightarrow{X}\rvert\notin\mathit{ff}(e)\cup\mathit{ff}(T)

(\mathbf{case}\;e_{1}\;\mathbf{of}\;T\to e_{2}\;\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to e_{3})\theta

\triangleq

\mathbf{case}\;e_{1}\theta\;\mathbf{of}\;T\to e_{2}\theta\;\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to e_{3}\theta

(T_{1}\;T_{2})\theta

\triangleq

(T_{1}\theta\;\;T_{2}\theta)

Appendix B
Complete Proof of the Substitution Lemma with Linear Implication Types

Lemma

(
Lemma
3.6
, Substitution Lemma)
.

If
\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash e:\tau
and

\Gamma\vdash G:\tau^{\prime}
, then

\Gamma\vdash e[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau
.

Proof.

By induction on the derivation tree of the typing relation

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash e:\tau
.
We split the cases by the rule used in the final step.

Case
Ty-Var
:
By assumption, we have a proof of the form

y[\overrightarrow{Z}]\in\mathrm{dom}(\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime})

Ty-Var

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash y[\overrightarrow{Y}]:\tau^{\prime}\langle\overrightarrow{Y}/\overrightarrow{Z}\rangle

and a proof ending with

\Gamma\vdash G:\tau^{\prime}
. The goal is to derive

\Gamma\vdash y[\overrightarrow{Y}][G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau^{\prime}\langle\overrightarrow{Y}/\overrightarrow{Z}\rangle.

1.

If
y=x
,
since we allow only one graph variable with the same name
in a single type
environment, we have
y[\overrightarrow{Z}]=x[\overrightarrow{X}]
and
\overrightarrow{Z}=\overrightarrow{X}
.
From the assumption
\Gamma\vdash G:\tau^{\prime}
, we
have
\Gamma\vdash G\langle\overrightarrow{Y}/\overrightarrow{Z}\rangle:\tau^{\prime}\langle\overrightarrow{Y}/\overrightarrow{Z}\rangle

using
Ty-Alpha
.
Since
y=x
,
y[\overrightarrow{Y}][G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]=G\langle\overrightarrow{Y}/\overrightarrow{X}\rangle=G\langle\overrightarrow{Y}/\overrightarrow{Z}\rangle
, which allows us to
rewrite the last typing relation to

\Gamma\vdash y[\overrightarrow{Y}][G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau^{\prime}\langle\overrightarrow{Y}/\overrightarrow{Z}\rangle
.

2.

If
y\neq x
, we have
(i)
y[\overrightarrow{Y}][G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]=y[\overrightarrow{Y}]
and (ii)

y[\overrightarrow{Z}]\in\mathrm{dom}(\Gamma)
from the premise of the above
Ty-Var
.
From (ii) we have

\Gamma\vdash y[\overrightarrow{Y}]:\tau^{\prime}\langle\overrightarrow{Y}/\overrightarrow{Z}\rangle
by
Ty-Var
,
which is the same as

\Gamma\vdash y[\overrightarrow{Y}][G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau^{\prime}\langle\overrightarrow{Y}/\overrightarrow{Z}\rangle
by (i).

Case
Ty-Arrow
:
By assumption, we have a proof ending with the following form.

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime},y[\overrightarrow{Y}]:\tau_{1}\vdash e_{1}:\tau_{2}

Ty-Arrow

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash(\lambda\,y[\overrightarrow{Y}]:\tau_{1}.e_{1})(\overrightarrow{Z}):(\tau_{1}\to\tau_{2})(\overrightarrow{Z})

Since we do not allow two or more graph variables with the same name
(though the name conflict could be circumvented by renaming),
we can assume
y\neq x
.

From the induction hypothesis on the premise of the above
derivation step

\Gamma,y[\overrightarrow{Y}]:\tau_{1},x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash e_{1}:\tau_{2}

and the assumption
\Gamma\vdash G:\tau^{\prime}
, we have

\Gamma,y[\overrightarrow{Y}]:\tau_{1}\vdash e_{1}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau_{2}.

By applying
Ty-Arrow
, we have

\Gamma\vdash(\lambda y[\overrightarrow{Y}]:\tau_{1}.\,e_{1}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]])(\overrightarrow{Z}):(\tau_{1}\to\tau_{2})(\overrightarrow{Z}).

Because
y\neq x
, we can move the substitution outwards and get

\Gamma\vdash(\lambda y[\overrightarrow{Y}]:\tau_{1}.\,e_{1})(\overrightarrow{Z})[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:(\tau_{1}\to\tau_{2})(\overrightarrow{Z}).

Case
Ty-App
:
By assumption, we have a proof ending with the following form.

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash e_{1}:(\tau_{1}\rightarrow\tau)(\overrightarrow{Z})

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash e_{2}:\tau_{1}

Ty-App

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash(e_{1}\;e_{2}):\tau

For the two premises of the above
Ty-App
,
the induction hypothesis gives us

\Gamma\vdash e_{1}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:(\tau_{1}\to\tau)(\overrightarrow{Z})

and

\Gamma\vdash e_{2}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau_{1}
.
From these,
Ty-App
get gives us

\Gamma\vdash e_{1}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]\;e_{2}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau.

Because

e[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]=(e_{1}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]\;e_{2}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]])
, we get

\Gamma\vdash(e_{1}\;e_{2})[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau.

and thus the lemma holds.

Case
Ty-Alpha
:
By assumption, we have a proof ending with the following form.

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash T:\tau_{1}

Y\notin\mathit{fn}(T)

Ty-Alpha

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash T\langle Y/Z\rangle:\tau_{1}\langle Y/Z\rangle

By applying the induction hypothesis to the first premise

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash T:\tau_{1}
, we obtain

\Gamma\vdash T[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau_{1}
.
Applying
Ty-Alpha
to this typing relation, we obtain

\Gamma\vdash T[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]\langle Y/Z\rangle:\tau_{1}\langle Y/Z\rangle
.

The remaining step to reach the final goal

\Gamma\vdash T\langle Y/Z\rangle[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau_{1}\langle Y/Z\rangle

is to prove

T[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]\langle Y/Z\rangle=T\langle Y/Z\rangle[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]].

This is proved by induction on the form of
T
. We focus on the
base case of
T
being a graph variable
y[\overrightarrow{W}]
because it is the
most non-obvious case that actually performs substitution,
whereas the structural induction steps are straightforward.

If
y\neq x
, the both sides are just
y[\overrightarrow{W}]\langle Y/Z\rangle
and the
claim holds trivially.

If
y=x
, the left-hand side is
G\langle\overrightarrow{W}/\overrightarrow{X}\rangle\langle Y/Z\rangle
,
while the right-hand side is

y[\overrightarrow{W}\langle Y/Z\rangle][G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]

=

G\langle\overrightarrow{W}\langle Y/Z\rangle/\overrightarrow{X}\rangle
.

By the definition of graph substitution,
\mathit{fn}(G)=\{\overrightarrow{X}\}
; therefore
it suffices to consider how each free link
X_{i}
in
G

is affected by the

\langle Y/Z\rangle
, for
1\leq i\leq|\overrightarrow{X}|
.
If
W_{i}=Z
, the link substitution applied to

G
behaves as
\langle Y/X_{i}\rangle
for both sides.
If
W_{i}\neq Z
, the link substitution applied to

G
behaves as
\langle W_{i}/X_{i}\rangle
for both sides. Therefore

G\langle\overrightarrow{W}/\overrightarrow{X}\rangle\langle Y/Z\rangle=G\langle\overrightarrow{W}\langle Y/Z\rangle/\overrightarrow{X}\rangle
.

Case
Ty-Cong
:
By assumption, we have a proof ending with the following form.

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash T:\tau

T\equiv T^{\prime}

Ty-Cong

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash T^{\prime}:\tau

By applying the induction hypothesis to the first premise
of
Ty-Cong
, we have
\Gamma\vdash T[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau
.

Structural congruence rules (
Figure

4
)
enjoy the following substitution property

T\equiv T^{\prime}\implies T[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]\equiv T^{\prime}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]],

which is straightforward by noticing that the requirement
\mathit{fn}(G)=\{Xs\}

of graph substitution ensures that the side conditions of (E6) and
(E10) on free links are not affected by graph substitution.

Now using
T[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]\equiv T^{\prime}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]
as the second premise of

Ty-Cong
, we get

\Gamma\vdash T^{\prime}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau.

Case
Ty-Prod
:
By assumption, we have a proof ending with the form

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash T_{1}:\tau_{1}

\dots

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash T_{n}:\tau_{n}

Ty-Prod

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),T_{1},\dots,T_{n},\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}):\alpha(\overrightarrow{W})

where

\alpha(\overrightarrow{W})\longrightarrow\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{n},\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V})\in P
.

By applying the induction hypothesis to the premise

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash T_{i}:\tau_{i}
, we have

\Gamma\vdash T_{i}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau_{i}
,
from which another application of
Ty-Prod
gives us

\Gamma\vdash\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),T_{1}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]],\dots,T_{n}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]],\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}):\alpha(\overrightarrow{W}).

From the definition of graph substitution,

\displaystyle(\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),T_{1},\dots,T_{n},\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}))[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]

\displaystyle=\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),T_{1}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]],\dots,T_{n}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]],\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}),

(143)

which allows us to factor out the substitution and get

\Gamma\vdash\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),T_{1},\dots,T_{n},\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V})[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\alpha(\overrightarrow{W}).

Case
Ty-Case
:
By assumption, we have a proof ending with the form

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash e_{1}:\tau_{1}

(\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime},\Gamma^{\prime})\vdash e_{2}:\tau

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash e_{3}:\tau

Ty-Case

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash(\mathbf{case}\;e_{1}\;\mathbf{of}\;T\to e_{2}\;\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to e_{3}):\tau

where each graph variable occurring
in
T
must occur with
a type annotation as

x_{i}[\overrightarrow{X_{i}}]:\sigma_{i}
,
and
\Gamma^{\prime}
= {
\overrightarrow{x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\sigma}
}.

By applying the induction hypothesis to the premises,
we have the following:

•

\Gamma\vdash e_{1}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau_{1}

•

(\Gamma,\Gamma^{\prime})\vdash e_{2}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau

•

\Gamma\vdash e_{3}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau
.

Using them as premises of
Ty-Case
, we have

\displaystyle\Gamma\vdash(\textbf{case}\ e_{1}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]\ \textbf{of}\ T\rightarrow e_{2}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]

\displaystyle|\ \textbf{otherwise}\ \rightarrow e_{3}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]):\tau

(144)

The definition of graph substitution allows us to factor out the
substitution and get

\Gamma\vdash(\mathbf{case}\;e_{1}\;\mathbf{of}\;T\to e_{2}\;\texttt{|}\;\mathbf{otherwise}\to e_{3})[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau.

Case
Ty-LI-Intro
:
By assumption, we have a proof ending with the form

Ty-LI-Intro

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}):(\overrightarrow{\tau}\multimap\alpha(\overrightarrow{W})){\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}}

where
\alpha(\overrightarrow{W})\longrightarrow\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{\tau},\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V})\in P
.
From this side condition and
Ty-LI-Intro
, we also have the following.

Ty-LI-Intro

\Gamma\vdash(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}):(\overrightarrow{\tau}\multimap\alpha(\overrightarrow{W})){\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}}.

Since
(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V})[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]=(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V})
, the above can be written also as

Ty-LI-Intro

\Gamma\vdash(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V})[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:(\overrightarrow{\tau}\multimap\alpha(\overrightarrow{W})){\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}}.

thus establishing the claim.

Case
Ty-LI-Trans
:
By assumption, we have a proof ending with the form

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash T_{1}:(\overrightarrow{\tau_{0}}\multimap\tau_{1}){\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}}

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash T_{2}:(\tau_{1},\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}}\multimap\tau_{3}){\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}}

Ty-LI-Trans

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash\nu\overrightarrow{V}.(T_{1},T_{2}):(\overrightarrow{\tau_{0}},\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}}\multimap\tau_{3}){\{\overrightarrow{W}\}}

where
\{\overrightarrow{W}\}=(\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}\cup\{\overrightarrow{Y}\})\setminus\{\overrightarrow{X}\}
.
By applying the induction hypothesis to the premises, we get the following:

•

\Gamma\vdash T_{1}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:(\overrightarrow{\tau_{0}}\multimap\tau_{1}){\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}}
,

•

\Gamma\vdash T_{2}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:(\tau_{1},\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}}\multimap\tau_{3}){\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}}
.

Applying
Ty-LI-Trans
to them give us

\Gamma\vdash\nu\overrightarrow{V}.(T_{1}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]],T_{2}[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]):(\overrightarrow{\tau_{0}},\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}}\multimap\tau_{3}){\{\overrightarrow{W}\}}.

From the definition of graph substitution, the graph substitution
can be factored out (without
\alpha
-conversion) and we get

\Gamma\vdash(\nu\overrightarrow{V}.(T_{1},T_{2}))[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:(\overrightarrow{\tau_{0}},\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}}\multimap\tau_{3}){\{\overrightarrow{W}\}}.

Case
Ty-LI-Elim0
:
By assumption, we have a proof ending with the following form.

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash T:(\emptyset\multimap\tau){\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}}

Ty-LI-Elim0

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.T:\tau

By applying the induction hypothesis to the premise, we get

\Gamma\vdash T[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:(\emptyset\multimap\tau){\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}}
.
Using this as the premise of
Ty-LI-Elim0
, we get

\Gamma\vdash\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.T[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau,

where we note that graph substitution does not change the set of free links.

Case
Ty-LI-Intro0
:
By assumption, we have a proof ending with the following form.

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash T:\tau_{1}

Ty-LI-Intro0

\Gamma,x[\overrightarrow{X}]:\tau^{\prime}\vdash T:(\emptyset\multimap\tau_{1}){\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}}

By applying the induction hypothesis to the premise, we get

\Gamma\vdash T[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:\tau_{1}
.
Using this as the premise of
Ty-LI-Intro0
, we get

\Gamma\vdash T[G/x[\overrightarrow{X}]]:(\emptyset\multimap\tau_{1}){\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}},

where we note that graph substitution does not change the set of free links.
∎

Appendix C
Removing Typing Rules on Linear Implication Types from Proofs

Our type system includes a transition rule,
Ty-LI-Trans
, and an elimination rule,
Ty-LI-Elim0
,
which allow a derivation to cancel a linear implication
and yield a judgement whose result type is not a linear implication type.
We show that, in typing graphs,
such cancellation is admissible:
any derivation that introduces a linear implication only to eliminate it subsequently
is inessential and can be transformed into one free of the linear implication fragment.
This situation parallels the simply typed
\lambda
-calculus,
where a term of base type, such as an integer,
admits a derivation without application or arrow-introduction rules.
Formally, we prove the following:

If a graph is typable at a type that is not a linear implication,
then there exists a typing derivation for that judgement
that does not employ any of the linear implication rules

Ty-LI-Intro
,
Ty-LI-Intro0
,
Ty-LI-Trans
, or
Ty-LI-Elim0
.

We note the following conventions.

•

We assume that molecules (e.g.,
T_{1},T_{2},T_{3},\dots
) are
left-associative.

•

Linear implication types are denoted with explicit braces as

(\left\{\overrightarrow{\tau}\right\}\multimap\tau)\{\overrightarrow{X}\}
.

•

According to
Definition

2.9
,
we assume without further notice that the free links of
the both sides of a typing relation are equal; that is, for any

\Gamma\vdash T:\tau
, we assume
\mathit{fn}(T)=\mathit{fn}(\tau)
.

We first give the relevant typing rules.

Ty-Prod

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T_{1}:\tau_{1}

\dots

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T_{n}:\tau_{n}

Ty-Prod

\Gamma\vdash_{P}\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V},T_{1},\dots,T_{n}):\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})

where

\bigl(\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})\longrightarrow\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V},\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{n})\bigr)\in P.

Ty-LI-Intro

\bigl(\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})\longrightarrow\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V},\overrightarrow{\tau})\bigr)\in P

Ty-LI-Intro

\Gamma\vdash_{P}(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}):(\left\{\overrightarrow{\tau}\right\}\multimap\alpha(\overrightarrow{X}))\{\overrightarrow{U},\overrightarrow{V},\overrightarrow{Y}\}

Ty-LI-Trans

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T_{1}:(\left\{\tau_{2},\overrightarrow{\tau_{1}}\right\}\multimap\tau_{1})\{\overrightarrow{X}\}

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T_{2}:(\left\{\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}}\right\}\multimap\tau_{2})\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}

Ty-LI-Trans

\Gamma\vdash_{P}\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(T_{1},T_{2}):(\left\{\overrightarrow{\tau_{1}},\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}}\right\}\multimap\tau_{1})\{\overrightarrow{W}\}

where

(i)

\{\overrightarrow{X},\overrightarrow{Y}\}\setminus\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}=\{\overrightarrow{W}\}

(ii)

\{\overrightarrow{X}\}\cap\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{2})
,

(iii)

\{\overrightarrow{X}\}\cap\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{2})
,

(iv)

\bigl(\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\cup\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}})\bigr)\cap\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{\tau_{1}})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{2})
,
and

(v)

\mathit{fn}(\tau_{1})\subseteq\{\overrightarrow{W}\}\cup\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{\tau_{1}},\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}})
.

Here,
\overrightarrow{\tau_{i}}
denotes
\tau_{i1},\dots,\tau_{in}

and is different from
\tau_{i}
.

These side conditions are used in the subsequent operations:
Conditions (ii), (iv), and (v) are applied in Hyperlink Creation Localisation (Step 2),
and Condition (iii) is used in Proof Tree Normalisation (Step 3)
to ensure that condition (ii) holds.

Ty-LI-Elim0

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:(\left\{\right\}\multimap\tau)\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}

Ty-LI-Elim0

\Gamma\vdash_{P}\nu\overrightarrow{X}.T:\tau

Because the both sides of a typing relation must have the same free links,

\mathit{fn}(T)=\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}
and

\mathit{fn}(\tau)=\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\setminus\{\overrightarrow{X}\}
.

Ty-LI-Intro0

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:\tau

Ty-LI-Intro0

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:(\left\{\right\}\multimap\tau)\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}

Because the both sides of a typing relation must have the same free links,

\mathit{fn}(T)=\mathit{fn}(\tau)=\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}
.

We review the admissibility of
Ty-Prod
in

\figref
fig:ty-prod-admissibility, which shows how a proof with

Ty-Prod
can be converted to a proof without it.
It is important to note that (i) the LHS of the linear implication
type of the right premise of
Ty-LI-Trans
is empty, and
(ii) the free links of its RHS and and the free links of the
linear implication type itself must be equal.
In the following discussion, we show how a proof tree that uses
typing rules with linear implication types can be transformed into one
that uses
Ty-Prod
instead by converting it into this form.

Ty-Prod
:

\bigl(\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})\longrightarrow\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V},\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{n})\bigr)\in P

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T_{1}:\tau_{1}

\dots

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T_{n}:\tau_{n}

Ty-Prod

\Gamma\vdash_{P}\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V},T_{1},\dots,T_{n}):\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})

Ty-Prod
derived from other rules:

\bigl(\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})\longrightarrow\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V},\tau_{1},\dots,\tau_{n})\bigr)\in P

Ty-LI-Intro

\Gamma\vdash_{P}(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}):(\left\{\tau_{1},\tau_{2},\dots,\tau_{n}\right\}\multimap\alpha(\overrightarrow{X}))\{\overrightarrow{U},\overrightarrow{V},\overrightarrow{Y}\}

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T_{1}:\tau_{1}

Ty-LI-Intro0

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T_{1}:(\left\{\right\}\multimap\tau_{1})\{\overrightarrow{Z}_{1}\}

Ty-LI-Trans

\begin{array}[b]{ccccc}\Gamma\vdash_{P}(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V},T_{1}):(\left\{\tau_{2},\dots,\tau_{n}\right\}\multimap\alpha(\overrightarrow{X}))\{\overrightarrow{Z}_{1},\overrightarrow{U},\overrightarrow{V},\overrightarrow{Y}\}\\
\ddots\\
\Gamma\vdash_{P}(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V},T_{1},\dots,T_{n-1}):(\left\{\tau_{n}\right\}\multimap\alpha(\overrightarrow{X}))\{\overrightarrow{Z}_{n-1},\dots,\overrightarrow{Z}_{1},\overrightarrow{U},\overrightarrow{V},\overrightarrow{Y}\}\end{array}

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T_{n}:\tau_{n}

Ty-LI-Intro0

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T_{n}:(\left\{\right\}\multimap\tau_{n})\{\overrightarrow{Z}_{n}\}

Ty-LI-Trans

\Gamma\vdash_{P}(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V},T_{1},\dots,T_{n-1},T_{n}):(\left\{\right\}\multimap\alpha(\overrightarrow{X}))\{\overrightarrow{Z}_{n},\overrightarrow{Z}_{n-1},\dots,\overrightarrow{Z}_{1},\overrightarrow{U},\overrightarrow{V},\overrightarrow{Y}\}

Ty-LI-Elim0

\Gamma\vdash_{P}\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V},T_{1},\dots,T_{n-1},T_{n}):\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})

Figure 18:
Ty-Prod
Admissibility

Theorem C.1

(
\textsf{Ty-LI-}\ast{}
Elimination)
.

Any typing derivation for a graph that uses only

Ty-Prod
and
\textsf{Ty-LI-}\ast

in the largest prefix of its derivation tree
that contains no premises of
Ty-Arrow

can be transformed
into one in which the typing uses only
Ty-Prod

and
Ty-Alpha

together with a single final application of
Ty-Cong
.

Proof.

We follow a proof tree (without the final
Ty-Cong
or
Ty-Alpha
)
upwards, repeating the operations described below, so that
we can construct a proof tree of a graph template without using

\textsf{Ty-LI-}\ast
.

If the original proof tree does not contain

Ty-LI-Elim0
, the claim holds vacuously because it does not
involve linear implication types at all.

If the original proof tree contains

Ty-LI-Elim0
, we can split the cases into the following
(i), (ii), (iii) based on the typing rule just above the
Ty-LI-Elim0
.
(Note that the conclusions of the other typing rules are not of linear
implication rules.)

(i) Case
Ty-LI-Intro0
:

If
Ty-LI-Elim0
is preceded by
Ty-LI-Intro0
,
since the free links of the both sides of a type relation is the same
in
Ty-LI-Intro0
, no hyperlinks are hidden by
Ty-LI-Elim0
.
That is, the proof tree is of the following form.

\begin{array}[b]{c}\vdots\\
\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:\tau\end{array}

Ty-LI-Intro0

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:(\left\{\right\}\multimap\tau)\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}

Ty-LI-Elim0

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:\tau

Because the premise of

Ty-LI-Intro0
and the conclusion of

Ty-LI-Elim0

are the same typing judgement,
we can simply remove those
Ty-LI-Elim0
and
Ty-LI-Intro0
.

\begin{array}[b]{c}\vdots\\
\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:\tau\end{array}

We repeat the same operation to the proof subtrees above this step.

(ii) Case
Ty-LI-Intro
:

If
Ty-LI-Elim0
is preceded by
Ty-LI-Intro
,
since the LHS of the linear implication type in the premise of

Ty-LI-Intro0
is empty, we have the following form:

\bigl(\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})\longrightarrow\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V})\bigr)\in P

Ty-LI-Intro

\Gamma\vdash_{P}(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}):(\left\{\right\}\multimap\alpha(\overrightarrow{X}))\{\overrightarrow{U},\overrightarrow{V},\overrightarrow{Y}\}

Ty-LI-Elim0

\Gamma\vdash_{P}\nu\overrightarrow{W}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}):\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})

Here, from the production rules and the link condition of

Ty-LI-Elim0
, we have
\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}=\{\overrightarrow{W}\}
.
Therefore, we can replace
\textsf{Ty-LI-Elim0},\textsf{Ty-LI-Intro}
by
Ty-Prod

to obtain a typing to a graph structurally congruent to the original:

\bigl(\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})\longrightarrow\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V})\bigr)\in P

Ty-Prod

\Gamma\vdash_{P}\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}):\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})

where

\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V})\equiv\overrightarrow{W}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V})
.

(iii) Case
Ty-LI-Trans
:

If
Ty-LI-Elim0
is preceded by
Ty-LI-Trans
,
by following the proof subtree above

Ty-LI-Elim0
towards upper left, one finds a series of one ore more

Ty-LI-Trans
’s followed by
Ty-LI-Intro
which terminates the
subtree, as in the upper part (before transformation) in

\figref
fig:prenex-trans.
Note that one cannot use
Ty-LI-Intro0
here because
the LHS of the linear implication type has one or more types.
In this case,
we first transform the derivation into its prenex normal form in Step 1.
Then, by repeatedly applying Step 2 and Step 3,
we obtain a proof tree in which, for each
Ty-LI-Trans
step up to
the left and uppermost
Ty-LI-Intro
,
the right premise has a linear implication type with an empty left-hand side,
and the right subtree ends with
Ty-LI-Intro0
,
as illustrated in
\figref
fig:ty-prod-admissibility.
Hence, this fragment can be replaced by a single
Ty-Prod
rule.
The same operation is applied recursively to the right proof subtree of

Ty-LI-Trans
as well.

Step 1. Prenex Normal Form Transformation:

First, we move the link creations of the graph to the leftmost of the term.
This transformation is carried out as shown in
\figref
fig:prenex-trans.
If an unintended variable capture might occur,
then such links should be
\alpha
-converted in advance
by applying
Ty-Alpha
above
the right premise of
Ty-LI-Trans
.
Since this yields a proof tree for a congruent graph,
we obtain the original typing relation by applying

Ty-Cong
at the very bottom.

This transformation is valid, that is,
it satisfies the side conditions of the typing rules.
The link conditions (i)–(iv) of
Ty-LI-Trans
are straightforward,
and condition (v) is established in
Lemma

C.2
.

Step 2. Hyperlink Creation Localisation:

We follow a sequence of
Ty-LI-Trans
’s from the bottom to upper
left, and
as long as linear implication type of the right premise has an
empty LHS, we transform the right subtree to the one that uses

Ty-LI-Intro0
and
Ty-LI-Elim0
as shown in

\figref
fig:hyperlink-hiding-localisations.
The boxes in the figure are provided merely for visual clarity.
In the transformation,
the boxed term
T_{i}
is replaced by
\nu\overrightarrow{Y_{i}}.T_{i}
,
so that the rules
Ty-LI-Intro0
and
Ty-LI-Elim0

can be introduced immediately after the boxed typing judgement

\vdash_{P}T_{i}:(\left\{\right\}\multimap\tau_{i})\{\dots\}
.

This localisation procedure stops when we reach the leftmost
uppermost leaf or when the right premise has a linear
implication type with a non-empty LHS.
We will show in
Lemma

C.4
that the graph templates
of the proof
trees before and after the transformation are congruent.
Hence, we obtain the original typing relation by applying

Ty-Cong
at the very bottom.

Step 3. Proof Tree Normalisation:

We follow the sequence of the
Ty-LI-Trans
’s towards upper left.
Suppose that each of the first to the
(m-1)
-th
Ty-LI-Trans
’s
has the right premise with
Ty-LI-Intro0
.
Suppose, for the
m
-th
\textsf{Ty-LI-Trans}_{m}
, the right premise has
a linear implication type with a non-empty LHS.

Then, by reordering the elements of the graph template, we can
reduce the number of types of the LHS of the linear implication
type of the right premise by the transformation shown in

\figref
fig:ProofTreeNormalization.
The transformation is repeated until the LHS of the linear
implication type of the right premise becomes empty.

The transformation step is explained in
\figref
fig:ProofTreeNormalization.
Before transformation,
the first (
m-1
)
Ty-LI-Trans
’s use
Ty-LI-Intro0
as their
right premises, and the
m
-th
\textsf{Ty-LI-Trans}_{m}
has an linear
implication type with a non-empty LHS.

The graph templates of the two conclusions are obviously congruent
and we obtain the original typing relation by applying

Ty-Cong
at the very bottom.
We will show in
Lemma

C.5
that the link condition
of all
Ty-LI-Trans
s are satisfied.
The above transformation is repeated until the LHS of the linear
implication type of the right premise of
\textsf{Ty-LI-Trans}_{m}
becomes empty.
When the LHS of the linear implication type of the right premise of

\textsf{Ty-LI-Trans}_{m}
becomes empty,
we apply Step 2 (Hyperlink Creation Localisation) to
\textsf{Ty-LI-Trans}_{m}
.

∎

\textsf{I0}_{1}

\vdash_{P}\nu\overrightarrow{Y_{1}}.T_{1}:(\left\{\right\}\multimap\tau_{1})\{\dots\}

\textsf{Tr}_{1}

E0

where

•

\{\overrightarrow{Y_{i}}\}=\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\setminus\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})

•

\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}=\mathit{fn}((T_{n+1},\dots,T_{i+1},\boxed{\nu\overrightarrow{Y_{i}}.T_{i}},\nu\overrightarrow{Y_{i-1}}.T_{i-1},\dots,\nu\overrightarrow{Y_{1}}.T_{1}))\setminus\mathit{fn}(\tau)=\{\overrightarrow{X}\}\setminus\{\overrightarrow{Y_{i}}\}

Here,

Ty-Prod

,

C.1
Lemmata

In this section,
we show that the transformations of proof trees in the proof of

Theorem

C.1
are valid;
they preserve the side conditions of the typing rules.

Lemma C.2

(Free Link Containment)
.

If
\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:(\left\{\overrightarrow{\tau}\right\}\multimap\tau)\{\overrightarrow{X}\}
holds,
then
\mathit{fn}(\tau)\subseteq\{\overrightarrow{X}\}\cup\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{\tau})
.

Proof.

By induction on the structure
of the typing derivation for linear implication.

Case
Ty-LI-Intro

By assumption, we have a proof of the form.

\bigl(\alpha(\overrightarrow{X})\longrightarrow\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V},\overrightarrow{\tau})\bigr)\in P

Ty-LI-Intro

\Gamma\vdash_{P}(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}):(\left\{\overrightarrow{\tau}\right\}\multimap\alpha(\overrightarrow{X}))\{\overrightarrow{U},\overrightarrow{V},\overrightarrow{Y}\}

Then, the lemma holds since

\mathit{fn}(\alpha(\overrightarrow{X}))=\bigl(\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\cup\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V})\cup\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{\tau})\bigr)\setminus\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}\subseteq\bigl(\{\overrightarrow{U},\overrightarrow{V},\overrightarrow{Y}\}\cup\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{\tau}))\bigr)
.

Case
Ty-LI-Trans

Since this property is precisely the link condition (v) of
Ty-LI-Trans
,
it is trivially satisfied whenever that condition is explicitly enforced.

Furthermore,
when we perform the transformation in
\figref
fig:prenex-trans,
and the graph typed by
Ty-LI-Trans
contains no leftmost hyperlink creation,
the property holds even when the link condition (v) of
Ty-LI-Trans

is not explicitly imposed,
as shown below.

By assumption, we have a proof of the form.

\begin{array}[b]{llll}\Gamma\vdash_{P}T_{1}:(\left\{\tau_{2},\overrightarrow{\tau_{1}}\right\}\multimap\tau_{1})\{\overrightarrow{X}\}\\
\Gamma\vdash_{P}T_{2}:(\left\{\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}}\right\}\multimap\tau_{2})\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\end{array}

Ty-LI-Trans

\Gamma\vdash_{P}(T_{1},T_{2}):(\left\{\overrightarrow{\tau_{1}},\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}}\right\}\multimap\tau_{1})\{\overrightarrow{X},\overrightarrow{Y}\}

By the induction hypothesis,
we have

\mathit{fn}(\tau_{1})\subseteq\{\overrightarrow{X}\}\cup\mathit{fn}(\tau_{2},\overrightarrow{\tau_{1}})

and

\mathit{fn}(\tau_{2})\subseteq\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\cup\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}})
.
Thus, the following desired property holds.

\displaystyle\mathit{fn}(\tau_{1})

\displaystyle\subseteq\{\overrightarrow{X}\}\cup\mathit{fn}(\tau_{2})\cup\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{\tau_{1}})

\displaystyle\subseteq\{\overrightarrow{X}\}\cup\bigl(\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\cup\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}})\bigr)\cup\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{\tau_{1}})

\displaystyle=\{\overrightarrow{X},\overrightarrow{Y}\}\cup\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{\tau_{1}},\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}})

Case
Ty-LI-Intro0

By assumption, we have a proof of the form.

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:\tau

Ty-LI-Intro0

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:(\left\{\right\}\multimap\tau)\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}

Since the free links of both sides of typing relation should be equal,

\mathit{fn}(T)=\mathit{fn}(\tau)=\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}
must hold
and thus

\mathit{fn}(\tau)\subseteq\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\cup\mathit{fn}(\textbf{0})
.

∎

Lemma C.3

(Subset Duality)
.

(A\cap C\subseteq B)=(A\setminus B\subseteq A\setminus C)
.

Proof.

The LHS and the RHS are translated to

(x\in A\land x\in C\implies x\in B)
and

((x\in A\land x\notin B)\implies(x\in A\land x\notin C))
,
which are equivalent.
∎

Lemma C.4

(Hyperlink Creation Localisation)
.

A graph with Hyperlink Creation Localisation as shown in

\figref
fig:hyperlink-hiding-localisations
is congruent to the original graph.

Proof.

Consider the proof tree illustrated in the upper part of

\figref
fig:hyperlink-hiding-localisations.
Its root rule is
Ty-LI-Elim0
.
The leftmost branch consists exactly of the rules
\textsf{Ty-LI-Trans}_{1},\dots,\textsf{Ty-LI-Trans}_{i}
.
In every such derivation step,
the left-hand side of the linear implication type in the second premise
is empty.

Here, the links
\overrightarrow{X}
are defined as

\{\overrightarrow{X}\}\triangleq\bigl(\mathit{fn}(T_{n+1})\cup\dots\cup\mathit{fn}(T_{1})\bigr)\setminus\mathit{fn}(\tau).

and the rule
Ty-LI-Intro
is applied at the top left,

T_{n+1}\triangleq(C(\overrightarrow{X}),\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}).

Then, the three side conditions on the links for
\textsf{Ty-LI-Trans}_{i}

are given as follows.
For all
1\leq j,k\leq n+1
,

\displaystyle j>i

\displaystyle\implies\mathit{fn}(T_{j})\cap\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})

(145)

\displaystyle j>i

\displaystyle\implies\mathit{fn}(T_{j})\cap\mathit{fn}(\textbf{0})=\emptyset\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})

(146)

\displaystyle i>k

\displaystyle\implies\bigl(\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\cup\mathit{fn}(\textbf{0})\bigr)\cap\mathit{fn}(\tau_{k})=\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\cap\mathit{fn}(\tau_{k})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})

(147)

By replacing
j,i
in (
145
) with
i,k
,
we obtain

\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\cap\mathit{fn}(T_{k})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{k}).

Substituting this into (
147
) for
\mathit{fn}(\tau_{k})
yields

\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\cap(\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\cap\mathit{fn}(T_{k}))=\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\cap\mathit{fn}(T_{k})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i}).

Hence, together with (
145
), we obtain

\displaystyle\forall j\neq i.\quad\mathit{fn}(T_{j})\cap\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i}).

Therefore,

\forall j\neq i.\quad\mathit{fn}(T_{j})\cap(\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\setminus\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i}))=\emptyset.

Let

\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\triangleq(\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\setminus\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})).

Then, the above can be rewritten as

\displaystyle\forall j\neq i.\quad\mathit{fn}(T_{j})\cap\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}=\emptyset.

(148)

By
Lemma

C.2
, we have

\mathit{fn}(\tau)\subseteq\mathit{fn}(T_{n+1})\cup\dots\cup\mathit{fn}(T_{i+1})\cup\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})\cup\dots\cup\mathit{fn}(\tau_{1}).

Hence,

\displaystyle\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\cap\mathit{fn}(\tau)

\displaystyle\subseteq\underbrace{(\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\cap\mathit{fn}(T_{n+1}))\cup\dots\cup(\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\cap\mathit{fn}(T_{i+1}))}_{\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})\;\because\eqref{C1}}

\displaystyle\qquad\cup\underbrace{(\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\cap\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i}))}_{\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})}

\displaystyle\qquad\cup\underbrace{(\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\cap\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i-1}))\cup\dots\cup(\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\cap\mathit{fn}(\tau_{1}))}_{\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})\;\because\eqref{C3}}

\displaystyle\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})

From this and
Lemma

C.3
, it follows that

\displaystyle\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\setminus\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\setminus\mathit{fn}(\tau).

(149)

Therefore, for links
\overrightarrow{X}
, we have

\displaystyle\{\overrightarrow{X}\}

\displaystyle\triangleq\bigl(\mathit{fn}(T_{n})\cup\dots\cup\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\cup\dots\cup\mathit{fn}(T_{1})\bigr)\setminus\mathit{fn}(\tau)

\displaystyle=\bigl(\mathit{fn}(T_{n})\setminus\mathit{fn}(\tau)\bigr)\cup\dots\cup{\bigl(\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\setminus\mathit{fn}(\tau)\bigr)}

\displaystyle\qquad\cup\dots\cup\bigl(\mathit{fn}(T_{1})\setminus\mathit{fn}(\tau)\bigr)

\displaystyle\supseteq{\bigl(\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\setminus\mathit{fn}(\tau)\bigr)}

\displaystyle\supseteq{\bigl(\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\setminus\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})\bigr)}

\displaystyle\because\eqref{C6}

\displaystyle={\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}}.

Let
\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}=\{\overrightarrow{X}\}\setminus\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}
.
From (
148
) and
\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\subseteq\{\overrightarrow{X}\}
, we obtain

\displaystyle\nu\overrightarrow{Z}.(T_{n+1},T_{n},\dots,T_{i+1},\nu\overrightarrow{Y}.T_{i},T_{i-1},\dots,T_{2},T_{1})

\displaystyle\qquad\equiv\nu\overrightarrow{X}.(T_{n+1},T_{n},\dots,T_{i+1},T_{i},T_{i-1},\dots,T_{2},T_{1}).

∎

Lemma C.5

(
Ty-LI-Trans
Link Condition Preservation)
.

Transforming proof trees as

\figref
fig:ProofTreeNormalization
preserves the link conditions
especially for
Ty-LI-Trans
.

Proof.

For the link condition (i) of
Ty-LI-Trans
, it holds trivially.
The link condition (v) of
Ty-LI-Trans
is established by
Lemma

C.2
.
Therefore, we focus on conditions (ii)–(iv) in the latter discussion.
For the link conditions of the rule
\textsf{Ty-LI-Trans}_{i}

in the transformed typing derivation in

\figref
fig:ProofTreeNormalization,
the following holds.

(ii)

\mathit{fn}(T_{m})\cap\mathit{fn}(T_{i})=\mathit{fn}(T_{m})\cap\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})

\quad\because\mathit{fn}(T_{i})=\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})
.

(iii)

\mathit{fn}(T_{m})\cap\mathit{fn}(\textbf{0})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})
.

(iv)

\bigl(\mathit{fn}(T_{i})\cup\mathit{fn}(\textbf{0})\bigr)\cap\mathit{fn}(\textbf{0})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})
.

For the link conditions of the rule
\textsf{Ty-LI-Trans}_{m}
,
the following holds.

(ii)

\mathit{fn}(T_{m+1})\cap\mathit{fn}((T_{m},T_{i}))\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{m})

because

•

\mathit{fn}(T_{m+1})\cap\mathit{fn}(T_{m})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{m})

holds by the link condition (ii) of
\textsf{Ty-LI-Trans}_{m}

in the previous proof tree.

•

\mathit{fn}(T_{m+1})\cap\mathit{fn}(T_{i})=\mathit{fn}(T_{m+1})\cap\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{m})

holds by the link condition (iii) of
\textsf{Ty-LI-Trans}_{m}

in the previous proof tree.

(iii)

\mathit{fn}(T_{m+1})\cap\mathit{fn}(\overrightarrow{\textbf{0}})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{m})

trivially holds.

(iv)

\displaystyle\mathit{fn}((T_{m},T_{i}))\cap\mathit{fn}(\tau_{m-1},\dots,\tau_{i+1},\tau_{i-1},\dots,\tau_{1})

\displaystyle=\bigl(\mathit{fn}(T_{m})\cup\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})\bigr)\cap\mathit{fn}(\tau_{m-1},\dots,\tau_{i+1},\tau_{i-1},\dots,\tau_{1})

\displaystyle\qquad\qquad\qquad\because\mathit{fn}(T_{i})=\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i})

\displaystyle\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{m})\quad\because\text{Condition (iv) of previous $\textsf{Ty-LI-Trans}_{i}$.}

For the link conditions of the rule
\textsf{Ty-LI-Trans}_{i-1}
,
the following holds.

(ii)

\mathit{fn}((T_{m+1},(T_{m},T_{i}),\dots,T_{i+1}))\cap\mathit{fn}(T_{i-1})=\mathit{fn}((T_{m+1},(T_{m},T_{i}),\dots,T_{i+1}))\cap\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i-1})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i-1})

\quad\because\mathit{fn}(T_{i-1})=\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i-1})
.

(iii)

\mathit{fn}((T_{m+1},(T_{m},T_{i}),\dots,T_{i+1})\cap\mathit{fn}(\textbf{0})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i-1})

trivially holds.

(iv)

\bigl(\mathit{fn}(T_{i-1})\cup\mathit{fn}(\textbf{0})\bigr)\cap\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i-2},\dots,\tau_{1})=\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i-1})\cap\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i-2},\dots,\tau_{1})=\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i-1})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{i-1})
.

For the link conditions of the rule

\textsf{Ty-LI-Trans}_{j}\quad(n>j\neq i)

the following holds.

(ii)

\mathit{fn}((T_{m+1},(T_{m},T_{i}),\dots,T_{j+1}))\cap\mathit{fn}(T_{j})=\mathit{fn}((T_{m+1},(T_{m},T_{i}),\dots,T_{j+1}))\cap\mathit{fn}(\tau_{j})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{j})

\quad\because\mathit{fn}(T_{j})=\mathit{fn}(\tau_{j})
.

(iii)

\mathit{fn}((T_{m+1},(T_{m},T_{i}),\dots,T_{j+1})\cap\mathit{fn}(\textbf{0})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{j})

trivially holds.

(iv)

\bigl(\mathit{fn}(T_{j})\cup\mathit{fn}(\textbf{0})\bigr)\cap\mathit{fn}(\bigl(\tau_{j-1},\dots,\tau_{1}\bigr)\setminus\tau_{i})=\mathit{fn}(\tau_{j})\cap\mathit{fn}(\bigl(\tau_{j-1},\dots,\tau_{1}\bigr)\setminus\tau_{i})=\mathit{fn}(\tau_{j})\subseteq\mathit{fn}(\tau_{j})
.

∎

C.2
An Example of the Elimination of
\textsf{Ty-LI-}\ast

We show how a graph (value) that is not of a linear implication type
can be typed without using the typing rules of
\textsf{Ty-LI-}\ast{}
,
using the following production rules as an example:

\displaystyle\mathit{list}(X)

\displaystyle\longrightarrow\mathrm{Nil}(X),

\displaystyle\mathit{list}(X)

\displaystyle\longrightarrow\nu W_{1}W_{2}.(\mathrm{Cons}(W_{1},W_{2},X),{\rm Nature}(W_{1}),\mathit{list}(W_{2})),

\displaystyle{\rm Nature}(X)

\displaystyle\longrightarrow\mathtt{1}(X),

\displaystyle{\rm Nature}(X)

\displaystyle\longrightarrow\mathtt{2}(X).

\Figref

fig:BeforeAfterTransformation-1
and

\Figref
fig:BeforeAfterTransformation-2 shows
transformations of a derivation tree.
The subscript
i
attached to symbols such as
\mathrm{Cons}_{i}

is merely for readability, to indicate the correspondence between constructor atoms
within the proof tree.
Similarly, the subscript
i
on type atoms such as
\mathit{dbllist}_{i}

marks those that will be cancelled,
so that the correspondence can be easily seen.

(1)
Before all the transformations:

\textsf{I}{}_{1}

\begin{array}[b]{llll}\vdash\mathrm{Cons}_{1}(W_{1},W_{2},X)\\
:(\left\{\cancel{{\rm Nature}_{1}(W_{1})},\mathit{list}_{2}(W_{2})\right\}\multimap\mathit{list}_{1}(X))\{W_{2},W_{1},X\}\end{array}

\textsf{I}{}_{1^{\prime}}

:(\left\{\right\}\multimap\cancel{{\rm Nature}_{1}(W_{1})})\{W_{1}\}\end{array}

\textsf{Tr}{}_{1}

\begin{array}[b]{llll}\vdash\nu W_{1}.(\mathrm{Cons}_{1}(W_{1},W_{2},X),\mathtt{1}_{1}(W_{1}))\\

\textsf{I}{}_{2}
