:(\left\{\cancel{{\rm Nature}_{2}(W_{3})},\mathit{list}_{3}(W_{4})\right\}\multimap\mathit{list}_{2}(W_{2}))\{W_{4},W_{3},W_{2}\}\end{array}

\textsf{I}{}_{2^{\prime}}

\begin{array}[b]{llll}\vdash\mathtt{2}_{2}(W_{3})\\

Appendix D
Proof of Propositions of Normal Forms

In this section,
We establish the existence and uniqueness of Normal Forms.

D.1
Existence of Normal Form

We first show
for any graph,
the typing derivation,
that is the largest prefix of its derivation tree
that does not contain premises of
Ty-Arrow
,
is derived solely by using

Ty-Alpha
,
Ty-Cong
,
Ty-Prod
, and
\textsf{Ty-LI-}\ast

(
Lemma

D.1
).

Then, we show
such typing derivation can be transformed
so that
Ty-Alpha
does not occur
and
Ty-Cong
occurs only once as the final rule
in the largest prefix of its derivation tree
that contains no premises of
Ty-Arrow

(
Lemma

D.2
,
Lemma

D.3
).

Then,
Any typing derivation for a graph that uses only

Ty-Prod
and
\textsf{Ty-LI-}\ast

in the largest prefix of its derivation tree
that contains no premises of
Ty-Arrow

can be transformed,
as shown in Appendix
C
,
into one in which the typing uses only
Ty-Prod
,

Ty-Alpha
, and
Ty-Cong
.

Applying the previous steps again,
we obtain the typing derivation
only consists of
Ty-Prod

for a congruent graph.

Lemma D.1
.

For any graph
G
,
the typing is derived solely by using

Ty-Alpha
,
Ty-Cong
,
Ty-Prod
, and
\textsf{Ty-LI-}\ast

in the largest prefix of its derivation tree
that does not contain premises of
Ty-Arrow

Proof.

We proceed by induction on the structure of the typing derivation.
Since
G
is a graph and not a case expression or an application,
the rules
Ty-Case
and
Ty-App
are not applicable.
As
G
is a graph and not a graph variable,
the rule
Ty-Var
cannot be applied.
Thus, only the rules

Ty-Alpha
,
Ty-Cong
,
Ty-Prod
,
\textsf{Ty-LI-}\ast
, and
Ty-Arrow

are applicable.
If one of

Ty-Alpha
,
Ty-Cong
,
Ty-Prod
, or
\textsf{Ty-LI-}\ast

is applied,
then its premises must be typing judgements of graphs,
by the definition of these rules.
Therefore, the claim holds by the induction hypothesis.
∎

Lemma D.2
.

Any typing derivation for a graph can be transformed
so that
Ty-Alpha
does not occur
in the largest prefix of its derivation tree
that contains no premises of
Ty-Arrow
.

Proof.

Since link substitution is defined compositionally for graphs,
the rule
Ty-Alpha
can be propagated upward
through the derivation tree.

When the transformation reaches a rule

Ty-Arrow
,
Ty-Prod
, or
Ty-LI-Intro
,
the application of
Ty-Alpha
can be eliminated at that point.

•

In the case of
Ty-Arrow
,
no restriction is imposed on the free links
of the
\lambda
-abstraction atom or the arrow type.
Hence, the resulting typing judgement
can be obtained directly without using
Ty-Alpha
.

•

For
Ty-Prod
and
Ty-LI-Intro
,
the link names in the applying production rule
can be freely renamed.
Therefore, the typing judgement after applying
Ty-Alpha

can be derived directly without using
Ty-Alpha
.

∎

Lemma D.3
.

Any typing derivation for a graph that uses only

Ty-Cong
,
Ty-Prod
, and
\textsf{Ty-LI-}\ast

in the largest prefix of its derivation tree
that contains no premises of
Ty-Arrow

can be transformed
so that
Ty-Cong
occurs only once as the final rule.

Proof.

We proceed by induction on the structure of the typing derivation.
Note that the number of rule applications strictly decreases.

Base Case.

Consider the case in which the typing derivation uses only a single rule.

In the typing derivation tree,
the only rules with no premises
are
Ty-Prod

whose production rule has no child types
and
Ty-LI-Intro
.
If the typing judgement
\Gamma\vdash_{P}G:\tau
is derived using only

Ty-Prod
and
Ty-LI-Intro
,
then by the reflexivity of structural congruence
G\equiv G
,
we can add
Ty-Cong
to derive the same typing judgement.

Induction Step.

We perform case analysis on the last rule used in the derivation:

Ty-Prod
,
Ty-LI-Intro
,
Ty-LI-Trans
,

Ty-LI-Intro0
,
Ty-LI-Elim0
, or
Ty-Cong
.

Case
Ty-Prod
.

Assume the last rule applied in the derivation is
Ty-Prod
.
By induction hypotheses the premises
can be derived using
Ty-Cong
only once at the end.
Thus, the following derivation can be obtained:

\vdots

\Gamma\vdash_{P}G_{1}^{\prime}:\tau_{1}^{\prime}

Ty-Cong

\Gamma\vdash_{P}G_{1}:\tau_{1}

\cdots

\vdots

\Gamma\vdash_{P}G_{n}^{\prime}:\tau_{n}^{\prime}

Ty-Cong

\Gamma\vdash_{P}G_{n}^{\prime}:\tau_{n}^{\prime}

Ty-Prod

\Gamma\vdash_{P}\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),G_{1},\dots,G_{n},\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}):\tau

Since
G_{i}^{\prime}\equiv G_{i}
,
it follows from structural congruence rules (e.g., E6, E7) that

\displaystyle\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),G_{1}^{\prime},\dots,G_{n}^{\prime},\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V})

\displaystyle\equiv\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),G_{1},\dots,G_{n},\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}).

Therefore, the following derivation is valid:

\vdots

\Gamma\vdash_{P}G_{1}^{\prime}:\tau_{1}^{\prime}

\cdots

\vdots

\Gamma\vdash_{P}G_{n}^{\prime}:\tau_{n}^{\prime}

Ty-Prod

\Gamma\vdash_{P}\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),G_{1}^{\prime},\dots,G_{n}^{\prime},\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}):\tau

Ty-Cong

\Gamma\vdash_{P}\overrightarrow{Z}.(C(\overrightarrow{Y}),G_{1},\dots,G_{n},\overrightarrow{U\bowtie V}):\tau

This derivation uses
Ty-Cong
only once at the final step,
and thus satisfies the lemma.

Case
Ty-LI-Trans
.

Assume the last rule applied in the derivation is
Ty-LI-Trans
.
By induction hypotheses the premises
can be derived using
Ty-Cong
only once at the end.
Thus, the following derivation can be obtained:

\vdots

\begin{array}[b]{llll}\Gamma\vdash_{P}G_{1}^{\prime}\\
:(\left\{\overrightarrow{\tau_{0}}\right\}\multimap\tau_{1})\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}\end{array}

Ty-Cong

\begin{array}[b]{llll}\Gamma\vdash_{P}G_{1}\\
:(\left\{\overrightarrow{\tau_{0}}\right\}\multimap\tau_{1})\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}\end{array}

\vdots

\begin{array}[b]{llll}\Gamma\vdash_{P}G_{2}^{\prime}\\
:(\left\{\tau_{1},\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}}\right\}\multimap\tau_{3})\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\end{array}

Ty-Cong

\begin{array}[b]{llll}\Gamma\vdash_{P}G_{2}\\
:(\left\{\tau_{1},\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}}\right\}\multimap\tau_{3})\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\end{array}

Ty-LI-Trans

\Gamma\vdash_{P}\nu\overrightarrow{X}.(G_{1},G_{2}):(\left\{\overrightarrow{\tau_{0}},\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}}\right\}\multimap\tau_{3})\{\overrightarrow{W}\}

Since
G_{1}^{\prime}\equiv G_{1}
and
G_{2}^{\prime}\equiv G_{2}
,
it follows from structural congruence rules (e.g., E6, E7) that

\nu\overrightarrow{X}.(G_{1},G_{2})\equiv\nu\overrightarrow{X}.(G_{1}^{\prime},G_{2}^{\prime})
.
Therefore, the following derivation is valid:

\vdots

\begin{array}[b]{llll}\Gamma\vdash_{P}G_{1}^{\prime}\\
:(\left\{\overrightarrow{\tau_{0}}\right\}\multimap\tau_{1})\{\overrightarrow{Z}\}\end{array}

\vdots

\begin{array}[b]{llll}\Gamma\vdash_{P}G_{2}^{\prime}\\
:(\left\{\tau_{1},\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}}\right\}\multimap\tau_{3})\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}\end{array}

Ty-LI-Trans

\Gamma\vdash_{P}\nu\overrightarrow{X}.(G_{1}^{\prime},G_{2}^{\prime}):(\left\{\overrightarrow{\tau_{0}},\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}}\right\}\multimap\tau_{3})\{\overrightarrow{W}\}

Ty-Cong

\Gamma\vdash_{P}\nu\overrightarrow{X}.(G_{1},G_{2}):(\left\{\overrightarrow{\tau_{0}},\overrightarrow{\tau_{2}}\right\}\multimap\tau_{3})\{\overrightarrow{W}\}

This derivation uses
Ty-Cong
only once at the final step,
and thus satisfies the lemma.

Case
Ty-LI-Elim0
.

Assume the last rule applied in the derivation is
Ty-LI-Elim0
.
By induction hypotheses the premises
can be derived using
Ty-Cong
only once at the end.
Thus, the following derivation can be obtained:

\vdots

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T^{\prime}:(\left\{\right\}\multimap\tau)\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}

Ty-Cong

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:(\left\{\right\}\multimap\tau)\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}

Ty-LI-Elim0

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:\tau

The above can be transformed as follows.

\vdots

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T^{\prime}:(\left\{\right\}\multimap\tau)\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}

Ty-LI-Elim0

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T^{\prime}:\tau

Ty-Cong

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:\tau

This derivation uses
Ty-Cong
only once at the final step,
and thus satisfies the lemma.

Case
Ty-LI-Intro0
.

Assume the last rule applied in the derivation is
Ty-LI-Intro0
.
By induction hypotheses the premises
can be derived using
Ty-Cong
only once at the end.
Thus, the following derivation can be obtained:

\vdots

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T^{\prime}:\tau

Ty-Cong

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:\tau

Ty-LI-Intro0

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:(\left\{\right\}\multimap\tau)\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}

The above can be transformed as follows.

\vdots

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T^{\prime}:\tau

Ty-LI-Intro0

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T^{\prime}:(\left\{\right\}\multimap\tau)\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}

Ty-Cong

\Gamma\vdash_{P}T:(\left\{\right\}\multimap\tau)\{\overrightarrow{Y}\}

This derivation uses
Ty-Cong
only once at the final step,
and thus satisfies the lemma.

Case
Ty-Cong
.

If multiple consecutive applications of
Ty-Cong
occur,
they can be merged into a single application.

\vdots

\Gamma\vdash_{P}G_{1}:\tau

Ty-Cong

\Gamma\vdash_{P}G_{2}:\tau

Ty-Cong

\Gamma\vdash_{P}G_{3}:\tau

Since
G_{1}\equiv G_{2}
and
G_{2}\equiv G_{3}
,

G_{1}\equiv G_{3}
.
Therefore the above can be transformed as follows.

\vdots

\Gamma\vdash_{P}G_{1}:\tau

Ty-Cong

\Gamma\vdash_{P}G_{3}:\tau

∎

4.15

(Existence of Normal Form).

Let
G
be a typable graph whose type is not a linear implication type.
Then, there exists a congruent graph
G^{\prime}

whose
typing derivation
uses only
Ty-Prod
in
the derivation
without premises of
Ty-Arrow
.

Proof.

By
Lemma

D.1
,
for any graph,
the typing derivation,
that is the largest prefix of its derivation tree
that does not contain premises of
Ty-Arrow
,
is derived solely by using

Ty-Alpha
,
Ty-Cong
,
Ty-Prod
, and
\textsf{Ty-LI-}\ast

Using
Lemma

D.2
and
Lemma

D.3
),
such typing derivation can be transformed
so that
Ty-Alpha
does not occur
and
Ty-Cong
occurs only once as the final rule
in the largest prefix of its derivation tree
that contains no premises of
Ty-Arrow
.

Therefore,
as shown in Appendix
C
,
Any typing derivation for a graph that uses only

Ty-Prod
and
\textsf{Ty-LI-}\ast

in the largest prefix of its derivation tree
that contains no premises of
Ty-Arrow

can be transformed,
into one in which the typing uses only
Ty-Prod
,

Ty-Alpha
, and
Ty-Cong
.

Applying
Lemma

D.2
and
Lemma

D.3
again,
we obtain the typing derivation
only consists of
Ty-Prod

for a congruent graph.
∎

D.2
Uniqueness of Normal Form

4.16

(Existence of Normal Form).

Let
G
and
G^{\prime}
be graphs in Normal Form such that
G\equiv G^{\prime}
.
Then
G
and
G^{\prime}
share the same typing derivation
among those that contain no premises of
Ty-Arrow
.

Proof.

As pointed out after
Definition

4.14
,
the syntactic structure of a graph in Normal Form can be viewed as a spanning tree,
where the nodes correspond to atoms and the edges correspond to
their primary root links.
Accordingly, the statement
is equivalent to claiming that the structure of this spanning tree is uniquely determined.

To establish the uniqueness of the spanning tree,
we traverse the primary root links of atoms in the graph,
starting from the free root link
X
of the type of the graph,
and demonstrate that the resulting traversal structure is uniquely determined.

When a graph
G
whose type has a link
X
as a root atom
is in a Normal Form,
it can be written in the following form:

\displaystyle\nu\overrightarrow{Y}.(C(\overrightarrow{Z},X),\overrightarrow{W_{1}\bowtie W_{2}},\overrightarrow{G}).

(150)

This representation arises due to two key factors:
the constraints imposed on type production rules by
Definition

4.5
,
and the fact that only the typing rules
Ty-Prod
and

Ty-Alpha
are used in the derivation.
The use of
Ty-Prod
ensures that the syntactic form of the graph conforms
to the structural constraints specified by
Definition

4.5
.
Although
Ty-Alpha
permits the renaming of free link names,
it does not affect the overall syntactic structure of the graph.

Due to the conditions on links in
Definition

4.5
,
specifically Conditions (3),
there is no atom in
\overrightarrow{G}
whose final argument is
X

except for
C(\overrightarrow{Z},X)

in
Equation

150
.
Therefore,
identifying the atom with final link
X
uniquely determines the first atom

C(\overrightarrow{Z},X)
.

By structural induction over the form of
G
,
it is straightforward to see that
every atom in
G_{j}
in
\overrightarrow{G}
is traversable via primary root
links from
Z_{i}
.
Also, any atom in
G_{k}
where
k\neq j
does not have a root link
Z_{i}

due to the link conditions in

Definition

4.5
(Conditions (3)).
Therefore,
we can uniquely determine which atom belongs to
which sub-spanning tree
G_{j}
for every atom in
G
.
Thus the partition of
G_{j}
’s is uniquely determined.

Also, since
Z_{i}
s are distinct by Condition (3)
in
Definition

4.5
,
The order of
G_{j}
’s is also uniquely determined.

Finally, the representation of
\overrightarrow{W_{1}\bowtie W_{2}}

is uniquely determined by the form of the production rules.

Therefore, Normal Form of any typable graph is uniquely determined
up to
\alpha
-conversion of links.
This implies that the spanning tree of the graph,
whose backbone consists of root links, is unique.
∎
